claim: For a set of peer items that would otherwise stack vertically and push everything below them down, use a horizontally swipeable card row so the group occupies one fixed-height band of the page.
why: On a narrow screen, vertical stacking consumes the scroll budget of the whole page; a horizontal track keeps the group's footprint constant and lets the user browse it without displacing the rest of the layout.
when: Within-page navigation through a collection of comparable items — recommendations, categories, media tiles — on mobile.
fails: Items must be compared side by side, or the set is small enough to show at once; horizontal tracks also hide content off-screen, so critical or one-off items should not live there.

claim: Never animate a swipe-driven transition with a linear easing curve; use an ease that accelerates in and decelerates out, with a slight overshoot for physical interactions like card snapping.
why: Nothing in the physical world moves at constant velocity — objects build and shed speed — so linear motion reads as mechanical and rigid. Momentum and settle make the interaction feel like it has mass.
when: Any positional or transform animation the user initiates by touch, especially carousel snapping and card releases.
fails: Continuous or ambient motion (loading spinners, marquees, progress) where constant velocity is correct, and situations where overshoot would visually collide with adjacent UI or fire twice on rapid repeated swipes.

claim: Choose the easing curve to express the product's intended tone: short duration with a hard decelerate for snappy/performant, springy with overshoot and settle for playful, long duration with gentle in-out for calm and premium — and apply that same curve family across the whole product.
why: Motion is read as personality before it is read as feedback; an inconsistent curve set makes a product feel assembled from unrelated parts.
when: Defining a motion system at the start of a project, or auditing an existing one.
fails: Tone must yield to task urgency — destructive confirmations and error states should not be springy or slow regardless of brand voice.

claim: Use the screen edges as a spatial device: skew, rotate, or scale cards down as they approach the left and right boundaries so the flat track reads as a curved ring of items rotating past the viewer.
why: A phone has no room for a wide track, but perspective distortion at the boundary implies depth and continuation, telling the user there is more content beyond the edge without adding UI.
when: Carousels where you want to signal a large or looping set and the items are visually simple enough to survive distortion.
fails: Cards contain text or controls the user must read or tap at the edges — skew and scale make those illegible and hard to hit.

claim: Always pair a swipeable track with a position indicator below it, and animate that indicator continuously with the swipe rather than snapping it after the gesture ends.
why: A swipe track hides both the size of the set and the user's place in it; an indicator that tracks the gesture in real time doubles as live feedback that the drag is being received.
when: Any horizontal carousel or paged view within a page.
fails: Sets large enough that dots become noise — then use a progress bar or count instead; a fluid indicator also needs a static fallback under reduced-motion preferences.

claim: Give the pagination indicator a fluid, magnetic transition — the active marker stretches toward and merges into the next dot as the swipe crosses the threshold — instead of a binary on/off highlight.
why: A morphing marker shows direction and partial progress mid-gesture, so the user can see whether releasing now will advance or snap back.
when: Carousels with a small number of pages where the indicator is a focal, brand-carrying detail.
fails: Dense indicator sets, or utilitarian UI where the extra motion draws attention away from the content it describes.

claim: Treat one screen edge as a horizon line: scale, fade, and compress items progressively as they travel toward it, so the collection reads as a spool of content receding into the distance rather than a flat list sliding off.
why: Depth cues make a bounded viewport feel like a window onto something larger, which reframes limited screen area as an asset instead of a constraint.
when: Browsing large or effectively endless sets where the goal is exploratory feel rather than precise selection.
fails: Selection tasks needing equal legibility across items — shrinking items biases the user toward whatever sits at full scale.

claim: When a gesture opens a full-screen or overlay mode, make the dimmed backdrop dismiss it by both tap and swipe, and make the dismissing swipe the inverse of the opening swipe.
why: Users retrace the gesture that got them in; supporting the reverse direction plus a tap on the empty area means no one gets trapped in the mode regardless of which mental model they hold.
when: Expandable cards, media viewers, sheets, and any mode entered by a drag.
fails: Modes with unsaved user input, where an accidental backdrop swipe would destroy work — require an explicit dismissal there.

claim: Every action reachable by a gesture must also be reachable through a visible control; ship the gesture as the accelerator, not the only path.
why: Gestures are invisible and undiscoverable — they reward users who already know them and strand everyone else, including users of assistive technology who cannot perform a drag at all.
when: Any destructive or primary action attached to a swipe, such as swipe-to-delete or swipe-to-archive in a list.
fails: Never in terms of accessibility; the tradeoff is only visual density, which is solved by putting the button behind an overflow menu or revealing it on the swipe itself.

claim: Design the swipe track so items retain velocity past the release point and decelerate into their snap position, rather than stopping the moment the finger lifts.
why: Carried momentum lets a single flick traverse several items, which is what makes long collections feel fast to browse; hard stops force one deliberate gesture per item.
when: Carousels and spools of more than about four items.
fails: Short sets or step-by-step flows (onboarding, wizards) where each screen must be seen — there, one gesture should equal exactly one step.

claim: Route page navigation through the same gesture the user already uses for scrolling or dismissing: make a swipe up on a card open that card's detail page, rather than requiring a separate tap on a button.
why: The gesture already carries a spatial meaning; reusing it means the navigation reads as continuing what the user was doing instead of interrupting it.
when: Detail pages reached from a card, tile, or list item in a feed.

claim: Make new content enter along the same axis and direction as the triggering gesture — a swipe up brings the next screen up from below, a swipe right brings it in from the left.
why: The user's finger sets an expectation of where things are going; motion that contradicts that direction reads as a cut, motion that agrees with it reads as one continuous movement the user caused.
when: Any gesture-initiated transition between screens or steps.
fails: Reverse navigation — going back should run the motion in the opposite direction, not repeat the forward animation.

claim: Build a screen transition as three concurrent layers rather than one animation: the tapped element scales up to fill the viewport, the background surface expands to fill the viewport behind it, and the new screen's content fades and translates in on top.
why: Separating the container from its contents lets the container establish the spatial move while the content arrives afterward, so nothing gets stretched or squashed and the eye has a stable shape to follow.
when: Expanding a card, tile, or thumbnail into a full page.

claim: Stagger the content's entrance slightly behind the container's expansion instead of animating both on the same timeline.
why: The container reaching its final size first gives the incoming text and controls a settled frame to appear in; simultaneous animation makes the content appear to be dragged along and reflowing.
when: Container-transform style page transitions.

claim: End an expansion transition with a small overshoot-and-settle at the leading edge rather than stopping flat at the target position.
why: A slight elastic settle signals momentum was carried through the gesture, which is what separates a physical-feeling transition from a linear tween.
when: Gesture-driven expansions where the user has supplied velocity.
fails: Frequently repeated or utility transitions, where a bounce on every navigation becomes tiring and slows perceived speed.

claim: Give a primary CTA in a linear flow two input modes: tappable for a normal press, and draggable so the user can push it toward the next step.
why: Offering the drag lets a confident user drive the transition themselves, and the drag is what makes the direction-following motion available in the first place.
when: Onboarding, wizards, and other stepped sequences with a single forward action.
fails: Destructive or irreversible actions, where an easy drag makes accidental commits likelier.

claim: Use an expanding shape mask as the transition device: grow a circle from the button far past the screen bounds to push the old content out, then swap in the next screen's circle and shrink it back down as the new content moves in.
why: The growing and shrinking circle is a single continuous form the eye tracks across the cut, so two separate screens read as one wrapping motion.
when: Step-to-step transitions in flows with a recurring anchor element like a next button.

claim: When designing a transition, mock it up zoomed out with the elements drawn outside the device frame so you can see the full paths, then crop back to the viewport.
why: Most of the motion in a mask or push transition happens off-screen; inspecting it only through the phone frame hides the mechanism and makes a simple effect look unbuildable.
when: Prototyping or reverse-engineering any transition where elements travel beyond the screen edge.

claim: If you can only afford one shared element, make it the image: have the thumbnail on the source screen scale and reposition into the hero image on the destination screen.
why: A single element persisting across the cut is enough to prove the two screens are the same subject, and it costs far less to build than a multi-layer masked transition.
when: Any list-to-detail or grid-to-detail navigation with a dominant image.
fails: Source and destination images with different crops or aspect ratios, where the mismatch shows as a visible jump or distortion mid-transition.

claim: Prefer transforming existing on-screen elements over sliding a whole new page over the old one.
why: A slide-over replaces the context wholesale and gives the user nothing to track; a transform preserves the link between where they were and where they now are.
when: Navigation between related screens — a list and its item, a step and its successor.
fails: Navigation between unrelated top-level sections, where no element is genuinely shared and a fabricated one would misrepresent the relationship.

claim: When a page has one strong 3D hero element, keep everything around it plain — minimal type, generous empty space, no competing decoration — instead of adding more visual treatment.
why: A moving 3D object absorbs almost all of a viewer's attention, so surrounding ornament adds effort without adding perceived quality, and competing focal points dilute the effect that is doing the work.
when: Landing pages or hero sections built around a single animated 3D centrepiece.
fails: Pages that must carry dense information or many equal-weight actions, where a dominant hero starves the real content of attention; also breaks if the 3D asset is low quality, since minimal surroundings leave nothing to compensate.

claim: Decompose a site you want to emulate into named components before opening any tool — e.g. 'centred logo rotating on its axis' plus 'text reel translating horizontally beneath it' — then rank them and build only the top one first.
why: Naming the parts converts an impression of a site into a concrete build list, and ranking them stops effort going into secondary elements before the element that defines the page exists.
when: Recreating or taking inspiration from an existing site or effect.

claim: Decide the output format the effect needs — looping video file, exported 3D scene, or embedded live canvas — before committing to a 3D tool, and confirm that format is available on the plan or licence you actually have.
why: Export capability is frequently the paywalled feature rather than the editing itself, so a tool can be fully usable right up to the point where it cannot hand you the asset you need.
when: Choosing between 3D or motion tools for a web deliverable.

claim: When picking a tool for an unfamiliar discipline, weight how closely its interface matches tools you already use; adopt the industry-standard heavyweight only when a constraint like cost or capability forces it.
why: Interface familiarity transfers directly into speed on the first project, whereas a more powerful tool spends that time on learning its model instead of on the design.
when: One-off or first-time 3D, motion, or effects work embedded in a larger web project.
fails: Ongoing or complex 3D work, where the deeper tool's ceiling and ecosystem outweigh the initial ramp-up cost.

claim: Ship a free-tool fallback path alongside the convenient paid one when the paid step is a single blocking feature rather than the whole workflow.
why: A single paywalled export step should not gate the entire result; an alternative route preserves the outcome and lets the cost/complexity trade-off be made deliberately.
when: Workflows where one stage of the pipeline is licence-gated.

claim: Hold one headline slot fixed and swap only the variable phrase inside it, so the sentence frame stays readable while the meaning changes.
why: Two pieces of copy occupy the same coordinates, so the reader parses one stable sentence and registers the change as content rather than as layout churn.
when: A headline whose grammar is a template — a fixed lead-in plus an interchangeable object or predicate.
fails: The alternate phrases differ enough in length or line count that the surrounding layout reflows on each swap.

claim: Repeat the swap at intervals down the page instead of firing it once in the hero.
why: A single hero animation reads as decoration; the same mechanic recurring becomes the site's structural signature and gives each section a reason to be scrolled to.
when: Long single-page scrolling sites with several sections of similar weight.
fails: Content-dense pages where readers scan for specific information and repeated motion in the reading column becomes an obstacle.

claim: Tie the swap to scroll position rather than a timed loop when the page is a scrolling narrative.
why: Scroll-triggered changes give the reader authorship of the transition, which reads as responsiveness; an autoplaying timer competes with reading and repeats whether or not anyone is watching.
when: Sections that enter the viewport one at a time as the user scrolls.
fails: Above-the-fold headlines seen without any scroll, where a timed cycle is the only way to show the alternates exist.

claim: When a swap coincides with a nearby illustration or loop, animate that element out and back in around the transition rather than leaving it static.
why: A brief exit and re-entry marks the moment as a deliberate beat and keeps the two elements reading as one composition instead of two unrelated animations.
when: A small mascot, icon, or looping graphic sits adjacent to the swapping text.
fails: The graphic carries persistent meaning — a logo, a status indicator, a navigation cue — where disappearing reads as a glitch.

claim: Reach for text swapping when the budget is one interaction: it turns a text-only page into an interactive one without adding imagery, 3D, or video.
why: The whole effect is type plus a transition, so it costs almost nothing to build yet supplies the movement audiences now expect from a considered site.
when: Minimal, typographically-driven pages, early portfolio work, or projects with no asset budget.
fails: Pages that already carry heavy motion elsewhere, where an extra moving line adds noise instead of interest.

claim: Make the swapped phrases carry voice — a joke, an admission, a shift in tone — not just a list of synonymous service words.
why: The mechanic draws the eye to that exact word, so the payoff has to be in the copy; interchangeable filler wastes the attention the animation buys.
when: Personal sites, studio pages, and brand headlines where personality is part of the pitch.
fails: Product or transactional interfaces where the swapped slot must state a fact precisely.

claim: When a hero image or video is visually weak and can't be reshot, animate its container shape or mask over scroll instead of replacing the asset — the motion carries the interest the frame doesn't.
why: A morphing mask changes what the viewer is looking at moment to moment, so attention comes from the transformation rather than from the quality of the underlying footage.
when: Stock footage, low-budget product shots, or generic imagery in a hero or feature block where the layout is otherwise finished.
fails: The image itself is the message (product detail, data, faces, editorial photography) — morphing the frame crops and distorts the thing the user came to see.

claim: End the morph on a composed frame rather than looping it — land the shape inside or against a large type block so the transition resolves into the layout.
why: A morph with a defined endpoint reads as choreography; one that just keeps deforming reads as decoration and stops rewarding attention.
when: Scroll-linked morphs in a hero or section transition where the media sits next to headline typography.
fails: Ambient background loops with no scroll anchor, where there is no defined end state to land on.

claim: Keep the geometric delta between morph keyframes small — nudge corner radii, aspect ratio, and clip-path points rather than transforming a full-bleed rectangle into a radically different silhouette.
why: Large shape changes force the browser to re-rasterise masks and re-composite large areas each frame, which drops frame rate and makes the motion read as stuttering rather than smooth.
when: Any clip-path, mask, or border-radius animation running on large media elements.

claim: Treat a morph as a legitimate page-entrance animation, not only a scroll effect — run it once on load so the first thing the visitor sees is the site assembling itself.
why: An entrance morph gives the page a memorable opening beat and signals craft before any content is read.
when: Portfolio and studio sites where first impression is the product.
fails: Utility apps and repeat-visit dashboards, where a replayed entrance animation delays task start every session.

claim: Judge a morph by reloading the page several times rather than by watching it once — if it stops feeling good on the second or third view, it is too long or too heavy.
why: The person building it sees the animation constantly while visitors see it once, so repeated viewing is the honest test of whether the duration earns its place.
when: QA of any entrance or one-shot animation.

claim: Animate morphs with compositor-cheap properties (transform, opacity, and simple clip-path/border-radius interpolation) and avoid re-laying-out the element mid-animation.
why: The stated failure mode is browser slowdown from the size of the change, which points at layout and paint cost rather than at the animation concept itself.
when: Implementing the effect in CSS or a scroll library on real media elements.

claim: When explaining a multi-stage process, render the full diagram statically first, then animate it stage-by-stage as the user scrolls, rather than animating on load.
why: The static state gives the viewer a map of the whole journey so they know how much is coming; scroll-driven reveal then paces the explanation to their reading speed instead of the designer's chosen timing.
when: Long-form marketing or explainer pages where a pipeline, workflow, or transformation has more than three discrete steps.
fails: Short pages or above-the-fold placements where there is no scroll runway to spend, and on content the user needs to scan or reference non-linearly.

claim: Tie diagram animation progress to scroll position, not to a timed autoplay, so the user controls the pace of the reveal.
why: The narrator scrolls slowly to absorb each stage — a scroll-bound animation lets any viewer do the same, and lets a fast reader skip ahead, whereas a fixed-duration animation forces one speed on everyone.
when: Sequential content where comprehension time varies widely between viewers.
fails: Users on scroll-jacked or touch-momentum contexts where fine scroll control is hard, and for anyone with reduced-motion preferences set.

claim: Give each animated stage of a process diagram an explicit named label that reads as a noun phrase describing the artefact at that point.
why: The narration works because every beat has a name to land on; motion alone communicates transition but not meaning, so the label carries the actual information.
when: Any diagram where the steps represent state changes to a single entity moving through a system.
fails: Purely decorative or ambient diagrams where naming parts would imply a precision the content does not have.

claim: Budget an animated diagram as a bespoke production, not as a component — assume it costs an order of magnitude more than the static version and only commit when the process it explains is central to the page's argument.
why: The effort is explicitly called out as prohibitive for most teams; the payoff only justifies itself when the process being explained is the product story rather than a supporting detail.
when: Deciding scope on a marketing site with fixed hours.

claim: If the full scroll-choreographed treatment is out of budget, ship the reduced version: animate the diagram in once on viewport entry, then add hover states on individual nodes.
why: Two levels of ambition are shown side by side and both are endorsed — entry animation plus hover interaction delivers most of the 'alive' feeling for a fraction of the choreography work.
when: Small teams or tight timelines that still want the diagram to feel considered.
fails: Touch-primary audiences, where hover states are unreachable and need a tap equivalent or must not carry essential information.

claim: On hover, focus a diagram by moving the hovered node into the primary position and blurring or de-emphasising its siblings, rather than only highlighting the hovered element.
why: Subtracting emphasis from everything else creates far more contrast than adding emphasis to one thing, and the rotation places the focus target where the eye already is.
when: Radial, circular, or clustered diagrams with several peer nodes competing for attention.
fails: Diagrams where spatial position itself encodes meaning — rotating the layout would destroy the relationship the positions communicate.

claim: Keep scroll-linked animation smooth by testing at realistic scroll speeds; choppiness reads as broken rather than as a stylistic choice.
why: The narration opens by noting animation looking a little choppy, which registers as a flaw the viewer notices before anything else about the effect.
when: Any scroll-driven motion, especially sequences with many simultaneously animating elements.

claim: Before shipping any animation, name the clarity or function it provides; if you cannot, delete it.
why: Motion without a job adds cost and distraction while communicating nothing; the speaker's own decorative portfolio animations are cited as a failure.
when: Any transition, hover effect, or entrance animation being added to an interface.

claim: When a horizontal navigation runs out of room for new links, collapse it into a menu that animates open rather than shrinking type or cramming items in.
why: The animation here has a real job — it reveals content that genuinely could not be displayed at once, so the motion carries information about where the links went.
when: Link count exceeds the available header width, on narrow viewports or link-heavy sites.
fails: Collapsing navigation that still fits comfortably hides primary destinations behind an extra click for no gain.

claim: On surfaces where browsing dominates over searching, reduce a persistent search bar to a compact trigger that expands into a full field on click.
why: Screen real estate should be allocated in proportion to how often a control is used; the expand animation makes the relationship between trigger and field legible.
when: Products where users mostly scroll and scan, and search is an occasional secondary action.
fails: On search-first products, where hiding the field behind a click taxes the primary task.

claim: Structure interfaces around progressive disclosure: show only what the user needs at this moment and reveal additional controls or content as the task demands them.
why: It keeps the default view uncluttered while keeping everything reachable, and it gives animation a legitimate role as the mechanism of reveal.
when: Any screen whose full set of controls or content would overwhelm the initial view.

claim: Default to a 'load more' button over infinite scroll for paginated lists and feeds.
why: Explicit pagination hands pacing control back to the user and keeps the footer reachable; infinite scroll continually pushes it out of reach.
when: Feeds, search results, catalogues, and any long list on a page that also carries footer content such as links, legal, or contact info.
fails: Contexts with no meaningful footer and a continuous-consumption model, where the trade-off shifts.

claim: Give buttons a small, brief animation on interaction as a near-universal default.
why: Micro-feedback confirms the press registered, which is functional rather than decorative.
when: Essentially all interactive buttons.
fails: When the animation grows large or slow enough to delay the resulting action.

claim: Avoid scrolljacking — overriding the browser's native scroll behaviour to drive an animation — except in rare, deliberate cases.
why: It seizes a control the user expects to own, which is the opposite of the control-preserving logic behind every other rule here.
when: Marketing pages and portfolios where cinematic scroll effects are tempting.

claim: Treat 'context matters' as a reason to check a pattern against the specific product, not as licence to ignore the defaults; state the contextual reason when you deviate.
why: The rules are offered as general defaults with named exceptions, implying deviation needs an argument rather than a preference.
when: Deciding whether a project is the exception to a stated interaction default.

claim: Build multi-step UI animations as a chain of duplicated frames where each duplicate changes only the properties that should animate, then link them with Smart Animate.
why: Smart Animate interpolates between matching layers across frames, so identical layer trees with one differing property produce a clean, predictable tween with no manual keyframing.
when: Prototyping state transitions in Figma — menus opening, panels expanding, items revealing.
fails: If the duplicate is restructured (layers renamed, reparented, or added) the matching breaks and elements pop in or cross-fade instead of animating.

claim: Animate reveals by keeping the element present in the layer tree at 0% opacity in the starting frame and raising it to 100% in the next frame, rather than adding or deleting the layer between frames.
why: A layer that exists in both frames can be interpolated; a layer that only exists in one has nothing to animate from, so it hard-cuts.
when: Fading in menus, tooltips, overlays, or any element that should appear as part of a state change.

claim: Restrict a prototype's trigger vocabulary to two interactions — hover for reveals and preview states, click for committed navigation — instead of picking a different trigger per connection.
why: A consistent trigger set makes the prototype feel like one coherent system and keeps the user's mental model simple as the flow grows.
when: Prototypes with many linked frames representing a single component's states.
fails: Hover triggers are meaningless on touch devices, so a hover-driven prototype cannot be validated as a mobile interaction.

claim: When a container and its children should animate in sequence, reveal the container first, then set the children to 0% opacity in that same frame so each child gets its own subsequent hover state.
why: Separating container entrance from child entrance produces staged, layered motion instead of everything arriving at once.
when: Menus, lists, or option panels where individual rows respond to their own hover.
fails: Staging too many steps makes the interaction feel slow and requires the user to hunt for each hover target.

claim: Duplicate frames with Option-drag (Alt-drag) to spawn the next state in place rather than copy-pasting, so the layer tree and naming stay intact for Smart Animate matching.
why: Duplication preserves exact layer identity, which is the precondition for property interpolation between frames.
when: Extending an animation chain by one more state.

claim: Align a revealed panel to the edge of the element that triggers it before setting its start state, so the fade happens in the final resting position.
why: Fixing position first means only opacity changes between frames; otherwise the panel slides and fades simultaneously, which reads as unintentional drift.
when: Flyout menus anchored to a sidebar or list row.
fails: When a deliberate slide-plus-fade is the intended effect, in which case the offset start position is the point.

claim: Attach the prototype connection to the specific element the user actually clicks (e.g. the button rectangle), not to the whole frame, so the interaction only fires from the intended hotspot.
why: Frame-level triggers fire on any click in the frame, which makes an intentional menu feel like it opens by accident; element-level triggers scope the interaction to the affordance the user sees.
when: A frame contains multiple interactive regions and only one should open a given panel or menu.

claim: Use Smart Animate as the transition whenever the source and destination frames share the same named layers, so matched elements tween instead of hard-cutting.
why: Smart Animate interpolates position, size, and opacity between layers with matching names, which is what converts two static frames into a single continuous motion.
when: Two states of the same screen differ only in the position/opacity/size of shared elements.
fails: Layer names or hierarchy diverge between frames — the matching fails and the transition degrades to an instant swap.

claim: Model an open/close menu as two frames connected in both directions: click on the trigger to enter the open state, and a hover-triggered link on an invisible element to control staying in or leaving it.
why: A single one-way link leaves the prototype stuck in the open state; the return connection gives the menu a defined exit and keeps the flow testable.
when: Prototyping any dismissible overlay — dropdown, quick-actions panel, flyout menu.

claim: Place a transparent (0% opacity) rectangle over the region you want to be hover- or click-sensitive and hang the prototype connection off that shape.
why: An invisible shape gives you an explicit, resizable hit area independent of the visible artwork, so the interactive zone can be larger or differently shaped than the graphic itself.
when: The visual element is too small, irregular, or made of multiple layers to serve as a reliable hotspot.
fails: The invisible rectangle overlaps other interactive elements and swallows their events.

claim: Choose 'while hovering' rather than 'on click' for connections whose purpose is to keep a state alive while the pointer stays over it, since the state reverts automatically when the pointer leaves.
why: Hover triggers are self-reverting, which reproduces the dismiss-on-mouse-out behaviour of real desktop menus without wiring an explicit close action.
when: Desktop or pointer-driven interfaces where menus should stay open only while the cursor is in range.
fails: Touch interfaces, where there is no hover state and the menu would be unreachable or never dismiss.

claim: To make Smart Animate produce a slide-in, duplicate the panel across both frames and shift its position by a small offset in the starting frame rather than adding a separate animation curve.
why: Smart Animate derives motion from the positional delta between matched layers, so displacement is the animation — the transition type does not need to change.
when: You want directional entrance motion (slide up, slide down) for a panel that is already being revealed by opacity.

claim: Keep entrance offsets small — a modest displacement is enough to read as motion; the exact number is not worth agonising over.
why: The point is to signal direction and give the eye something to follow, not to travel a measured distance; large offsets read as sluggish or distracting.
when: Menus, dropdowns, tooltips, and other small overlay elements entering the screen.
fails: Full-screen or large panels, where a tiny offset is imperceptible and a full off-canvas position is the right starting point.

claim: Preview the prototype as soon as the basic connections are in place, then layer on polish like motion offsets in a second pass.
why: Verifying that the triggers fire correctly before adding motion isolates wiring bugs from animation bugs and gives a working baseline to compare the refinement against.
when: Building any multi-state interactive prototype.

claim: Give an element the exact same layer name in both the start and end frames of a Smart Animate transition; if the names differ, the transition degrades from a morph to a cross-fade.
why: Smart Animate pairs layers across frames by name match, not by position or visual similarity. A matched pair is treated as one object whose properties are interpolated; an unmatched pair is treated as two unrelated objects, so one fades out while the other fades in.
when: Any prototype where a shape should visibly move, resize, or change colour between two states — a search bar expanding into a panel, a card growing into a detail view, a pill sliding between nav items.
fails: You actually want a cross-fade or a hard swap between two conceptually different elements — in that case matching names forces an unwanted morph. It also misfires when two unrelated layers coincidentally share a name, causing an element to fly across the screen to an unintended target.

claim: Build each new prototype state by duplicating the previous frame rather than assembling it from scratch.
why: The duplicate inherits every layer name, position, and style from the source frame, so all the shared chrome is already name-matched and will animate correctly; only the differing content needs editing.
when: Multi-state prototypes where consecutive states share most of their structure, such as a sidebar with several selectable items.
fails: States that share almost nothing structurally — duplicating then leaves a pile of stale layers to clean up, and it can silently carry over names you meant to break.

claim: When swapping the contents of a container between states, delete only the inner content and keep the container layer itself.
why: The surviving container keeps its identity and name across both frames, so Smart Animate animates its size and position change; deleting and redrawing it creates a new object that can only fade.
when: Panels, cards, popovers, and modals whose frame persists visually while the payload inside changes.
fails: The container is meant to appear or disappear entirely between the two states, where persistence is not the goal.

claim: After dropping new content into a persistent container, resize the container to fit that content before wiring up the transition.
why: The size difference between the two frames is what produces the growth or expansion animation, and a container left at its old height either clips the content or leaves dead space in the final state.
when: Any state change where the payload's height or width differs from the previous state's.

claim: Establish one canonical name per persistent element and copy it verbatim between frames rather than retyping it.
why: Name matching is exact-string; a typo, trailing space, or capitalisation difference is invisible in the layer list but silently breaks the morph, producing a fade that is hard to trace back to its cause.
when: Whenever you rename a layer specifically to make it match a counterpart in another frame.

claim: Preview the transition immediately after connecting each pair of frames, before building the next one.
why: The animation is the only reliable feedback that the naming and geometry are correct; validating one state at a time keeps a broken transition from being replicated across every duplicate that follows.
when: Iterative multi-state prototypes built by duplication.

claim: Once a two-frame transition works for one item in a repeating set, replicate that exact process for the remaining items rather than inventing a different mechanism per item.
why: Consistent construction gives consistent motion across the whole component, and a validated pattern is cheaper to repeat than to redesign.
when: Navigation menus, tab bars, filter lists — any set of peer elements that should behave identically.

claim: To make one element visually become another (a rectangle becoming a search bar), keep it as the same layer across both frames and change only its size, position and styling — do not delete it and draw a new shape.
why: Smart animate matches layers between frames by identity/name; a re-drawn shape has no counterpart to interpolate from, so it pops in instead of morphing.
when: Any two-frame transition where a shape should appear to transform, expand or travel into a new role in the layout.
fails: Breaks if the layers are renamed, re-created, or moved into a different parent between frames — matching fails and the transition falls back to a hard cut.

claim: Build enter animations as a two-frame diff: duplicate the finished frame, then on the 'before' copy push the entering elements a small distance down and set their opacity to 0. Leave the 'after' frame untouched.
why: The transition engine tweens the delta between the two states, so a position offset plus an opacity delta produces a slide-up-and-fade-in for free, with no keyframes to author.
when: Content that should reveal itself as part of a state change — labels appearing when a collapsed sidebar expands, panel contents loading in.
fails: Offsetting too far turns a subtle reveal into a distracting flight path; the offset should be a nudge (roughly the element's own height or less), not a screen-length move.

claim: Give each element in a sequenced transition a small delay rather than starting them all at t=0.
why: Staggered starts make a compound transition read as one choreographed motion with a direction of travel; simultaneous starts read as a single flat jump.
when: A state change where several elements move or fade at once — a panel expanding while its contents populate.
fails: Delays that accumulate past a few hundred milliseconds make the interface feel unresponsive to the click that triggered it.

claim: Set the trigger explicitly on every connection in a chained click-through flow, not just the first one.
why: An unset or mismatched trigger silently breaks the chain at that link, and the prototype dead-ends at the frame before it.
when: Multi-step prototypes where one interaction leads into a sequence of frames.

claim: When a collapsed, icon-only navigation expands, pair every icon with a text label in the expanded state.
why: Icons alone are ambiguous outside of a handful of universal glyphs; the extra width earned by expanding should be spent on naming the destinations.
when: Expandable sidebars, rails, and any collapse/expand navigation pattern.
fails: Not a reason to label icons in the collapsed state — there the icon carries the meaning and a label would defeat the collapse.

claim: Mark the active or hovered row in a sidebar with a fill only a shade off the background — barely off-white on white — rather than a saturated highlight.
why: The row needs to be distinguishable, not dominant; a low-contrast plate separates it from its neighbours without competing with the content area for attention.
when: List and nav rows that need selected, hovered or active states inside a chrome surface.
fails: Too subtle a shift can fall below perceptible contrast on low-quality displays or in bright light, so the state should not be carried by the fill alone if it is the only affordance.

claim: Prototype the transition in preview as soon as it is wired, before layering the next element into the sequence.
why: Motion cannot be judged from the static frames; timing and direction only reveal themselves in playback, and errors compound if several transitions are stacked before the first is checked.
when: Any multi-step animated prototype built frame by frame.

claim: Wire hover states with a while-hovering trigger between two near-identical frames rather than a click or tap trigger, so the state reverts automatically when the cursor leaves.
why: While-hovering is a held state: entering plays forward, leaving plays back, which matches how a real hover behaves without needing a second return connection.
when: Any pointer-driven affordance in a desktop prototype — sidebar icons, nav items, buttons.
fails: Touch-first designs, where there is no hover; the state either never fires or gets stuck on tap.

claim: Apply the same hover treatment to every item in a repeated set, not just the one you are demoing.
why: Partial interactivity breaks the illusion — a user who hovers a neighbouring icon and gets nothing reads the whole prototype as broken.
when: Icon rails, nav lists, card grids, and any repeated component group in a clickable prototype.
fails: Deliberately disabled or non-interactive items, which should stay inert to signal their state.

claim: Build each new prototype state by duplicating the previous frame and changing only the properties that differ, instead of composing a fresh frame.
why: Shared layer names and positions between frames are what let the transition interpolate smoothly, and it guarantees everything unrelated stays pixel-identical across states.
when: Multi-state flows where consecutive screens are variations of one layout.
fails: Genuinely different screens; duplicating there carries dead layers forward and bloats the file.

claim: After duplicating a frame, explicitly reset any transient state you had applied — return hover opacity to zero and the surface back to its base colour — before building the next state on top.
why: A duplicate inherits whatever interaction state was left visible, so the next screen silently starts from a hovered or highlighted baseline and the transition into it looks wrong.
when: Any time a duplicated frame becomes the resting state of the following step.

claim: Mark the focused or active item with a coloured stroke plus increased stroke weight, rather than colour alone.
why: Two coincident signals make the active item unmistakable at a glance and keep it legible when colour is desaturated or the item sits on a busy backdrop.
when: Selection, focus, and active-item states in lists, cards, and sidebars.
fails: Layouts with tight spacing, where a heavier stroke expands the visual bounds and shifts neighbouring elements or crowds the gutter.

claim: When one element takes focus, push the surrounding surface back with a layer blur of roughly 24px on the backdrop rather than dimming it with an overlay.
why: Blur removes competing detail while preserving the sense that the context is still there, so the focused element reads as elevated instead of the background reading as switched off.
when: Modals, focused cards, spotlight or command-palette moments over an existing layout.
fails: Performance-sensitive real implementations, or when the blurred content still needs to be read; blur also fails as the only signal if the focused element has no elevation of its own.

claim: Animate an icon into a text button on hover by placing the icon in the resting frame at zero opacity, scaled down, and overlapping the label — then in the hover frame restore it to full size, full opacity, and its own slot with the label nudged aside.
why: Keeping the icon present in both frames lets the transition interpolate scale, opacity, and position into one continuous grow-and-settle motion instead of a pop-in.
when: Button and link hover affordances where an icon should appear alongside existing text.
fails: When the label shifts far enough that the text jumps — reserve the space, or the motion reads as a layout reflow rather than a reveal.

claim: Scale a duplicated element with the scale tool rather than dragging its bounding box.
why: Scaling resizes strokes, corner radii, and nested spacing proportionally, so the shrunken copy is a true miniature of its full-size counterpart and interpolates cleanly between states.
when: Preparing the small-state version of an icon or component for a grow-in animation.

claim: Attach the interaction to the container rectangle behind an element, not to the label or icon itself.
why: The rectangle defines the full clickable and hoverable area, so the state fires anywhere in the visual target instead of only on the glyph's own bounds.
when: Any button, row, or card whose visible hit area is larger than its content.

claim: Resize the container to fit newly pasted content before wiring any transitions.
why: Layout corrections after the connections exist force you to re-check every state; sizing first keeps the frames aligned so the transition does not reveal a jump.
when: Adding content into a duplicated state frame.

claim: Run the prototype immediately after wiring each interaction rather than batching all the connections and testing at the end.
why: Each connection is cheap to test in isolation, and a wrong trigger or target is far easier to find before more links are stacked on top of it.
when: Building any multi-step interactive prototype.

claim: To build a new screen state, duplicate the nearest existing screen, delete only the content region, and paste the new content into the same shell — do not rebuild the frame from scratch.
why: The duplicate inherits frame size, background, padding, and any shared chrome, so every state in the flow stays pixel-consistent without re-specifying styles.
when: Adding another state to a flow whose container and chrome are already settled.
fails: The new state genuinely changes the container (different size, different chrome), where inherited properties become leftovers you have to hunt down.

claim: Animate a continuous spin by chaining duplicate frames that step the icon's rotation by 180° at a time, rather than setting a single 360° rotation on one transition.
why: A tweened transition interpolates between two states; a 0°→360° change has no visible difference to interpolate, so the icon sits still. Half-turns give the engine an unambiguous direction to travel each hop.
when: Building a loading, syncing, or refreshing indicator that must rotate continuously in a click-through prototype.
fails: You need precise easing or a truly infinite loop — a fixed chain of frames only spins for as many hops as you build.

claim: Alternate the transform across the chain — rest, rotated, rest, rotated, rest — so each frame differs from its neighbour by exactly one half-turn.
why: Every consecutive pair must contain a change or that hop renders as a dead beat; alternating guarantees each transition carries exactly one 180° increment and the icon returns to its start orientation on a whole number of turns.
when: Sequencing any repeating cyclical motion out of discrete prototype frames.
fails: Two adjacent frames end up identical, which stalls the animation for one step's duration.

claim: Duplicate the full set of loop frames up front, then edit only the transform on each — keep every other property identical across the chain.
why: Tweened transitions animate whatever differs between frames; an accidental position or size change on one duplicate injects a visible jolt into what should be pure rotation.
when: Any frame-by-frame animation built from duplicates.

claim: Use a click trigger on the element the user actually presses to enter the loading state, but drag the connection from the frame itself — not from a layer — for the automatic hops inside the loop.
why: A frame-level connection fires without user input, which is what an unattended loading sequence needs; layer-level connections wait for interaction.
when: Distinguishing user-initiated navigation from time-driven state progression in a prototype.

claim: Model a loading state as its own dedicated screen sitting between the user's action and the result, not as an overlay improvised at demo time.
why: Giving the wait its own frame forces you to design what the user actually sees during it and makes the delay legible in the prototype flow.
when: Prototyping any flow with a submit, save, or fetch step.

claim: Give staggered elements in a loop or loader animation a per-element delay (~300ms scale) rather than firing them all at the same instant, so the sequence reads as motion travelling around the group.
why: Identical simultaneous transitions read as a single pulse; offsetting the start times is what creates the perceived rotation or wave.
when: Building spinners, skeleton shimmers, or any repeating multi-element loading indicator from discrete frames.
fails: Delays large enough that the last element starts after the first has finished make the group look disconnected rather than continuous; for a smooth loop, total stagger should stay within the cycle duration.

claim: Use built-in easing presets by default and reserve hand-tuned spring curves for the one or two moments where the default motion is visibly wrong.
why: Custom curves are a maintenance and consistency cost; keeping them rare means the whole file shares one motion feel and the exception carries deliberate emphasis.
when: Any multi-step prototype or motion system with many transitions.

claim: For a snappy, tight loader tick, use a high-stiffness low-damping spring — around stiffness 550, damping 40, mass left at the default — instead of a slow eased curve.
why: High stiffness gives a fast attack and low damping leaves just enough overshoot for the element to feel alive rather than mechanical, which is what makes each step of a spinner pop.
when: Short, small-travel transitions on repeated indicator elements.
fails: Applying the same aggressive spring to large moving surfaces (panels, sheets, page transitions) makes the overshoot look unstable; those need higher damping or lower stiffness.

claim: Apply the identical delay and curve settings to every element in a repeating set so the only variable between them is their position in the sequence.
why: Uniform timing is what makes a stagger read as one coherent motion; mixed curves make the loop stutter.
when: Any set of sibling elements animating as one group.

claim: Build a new state by duplicating the previous frame, deleting only the state-specific content, and pasting the new content into the same frame — never by drawing a fresh frame from scratch.
why: Duplication preserves frame size, position, and every shared layer's name and structure, which is exactly what the tweening engine needs to match elements between states.
when: Creating success, error, empty, or any follow-on state that shares a container with the previous one.

claim: Ensure any layer that should morph between two states carries byte-identical names in both frames, otherwise Smart Animate treats it as two unrelated layers and cross-fades instead of tweening.
why: Smart Animate pairs layers by name, not by visual similarity or position; a renamed or auto-numbered duplicate silently breaks the tween.
when: Transitioning between frames with shared icons, containers, or text elements.
fails: Name matching is not enough when the layers sit at different depths in the layer tree — matching names must also live in matching parent structures.

claim: Preview the prototype after each timing change rather than configuring every transition first, since spring and delay values can only be judged in motion.
why: Numeric stiffness and damping values have no reliable visual meaning on paper; the only test is whether the loop feels right at speed.
when: Tuning motion in any prototyping tool.

claim: When you want an element to slide into view rather than fade, wrap it in a mask sized to its container instead of animating opacity; move the element outside the mask in the start frame and inside it in the end frame.
why: Smart-animate style transitions interpolate position, and the mask clips anything outside its bounds, so the same positional tween reads as the element entering through a hard edge rather than materialising in place.
when: Frame-to-frame prototypes where a small indicator (check, arrow, badge) should appear inside a bounded shape.
fails: If the element must remain visible outside the container, or if the prototype uses a transition that does not interpolate layer position — the masked copy will simply pop.

claim: Build the mask shape by duplicating the container's exact dimensions and corner radius, not by eyeballing a rectangle.
why: A mask whose edge does not coincide with the visible container edge produces a clip line that reads as a rendering bug — the mark appears or vanishes at the wrong boundary.
when: Any mask meant to be invisible, where the clipping edge should coincide with an existing shape's silhouette.
fails: When the mask is intentionally offset to create a partial reveal or a directional wipe.

claim: Order the mask shape below the content it clips, then select the mask plus all clipped layers together before applying the mask operation.
why: Mask operations consume the bottom-most selected layer as the mask and apply it upward; wrong stacking order either masks nothing or hides the wrong layer.
when: Applying 'use as mask' in Figma or an equivalent clipping group in any layered editor.

claim: Author the animation's end state first with everything in its final position, then copy that group into the start frame and displace the moving parts — do not build the two states independently.
why: Copying guarantees identical layer names and structure across frames, which is what lets the prototype engine match layers and tween them instead of cross-dissolving.
when: Two-frame smart-animate transitions where the same object must be recognised in both frames.
fails: If the two states genuinely contain different objects, matching will fail regardless of copy order and you need explicit naming discipline instead.

claim: In a selected state, reserve the accent colour for the indicator itself and neutralise the container stroke.
why: Two accent-coloured elements in the same component compete; demoting the frame lets the newly arriving mark carry the meaning of 'selected'.
when: Designing active/selected variants of nav items, checkboxes, or toggles that gain an internal indicator.
fails: When the container stroke is the sole selection cue and no interior mark exists.

claim: Hide the pre-animation element by moving it out of the mask's bounds rather than by setting opacity to zero or toggling visibility.
why: A hidden or zero-opacity layer gives the transition nothing to travel from, collapsing the motion back into a fade; a displaced layer preserves a position delta to interpolate.
when: Any entrance animation built from positional interpolation between two frames.
fails: When the intended entrance really is a fade or scale, where opacity/size deltas are the correct authoring tool.

claim: Complete every visual state before entering prototyping mode, and add connections as the last step.
why: Prototype links reference frames and layer structure; restructuring layers after wiring risks breaking the matching that the transition depends on.
when: Multi-frame interactive prototypes assembled by hand.

claim: When staggering interface animations, express the offset as a short delay (on the order of a few hundred milliseconds) on the later element rather than lengthening its duration, so elements arrive in sequence while each individual move stays quick.
why: A delay shifts when a move starts without slowing the move itself, which keeps the sequence readable as cause-and-effect without making the interface feel sluggish.
when: Coordinating two or more elements that should animate in a visible order, such as a sidebar panel and the content or labels that follow it.
fails: Chaining many delayed steps, where the accumulated wait makes the interface feel unresponsive; also unsuitable for direct-manipulation feedback that must start on the same frame as the input.

claim: Return non-standard easing curves to your project's default (typically an ease-out) once you've finished the effect that required them, so exceptional curves stay exceptional and the rest of the prototype animates consistently.
why: A single default curve gives the whole prototype one motion character; deviations then read as deliberate emphasis instead of noise.
when: Building a multi-step prototype where you temporarily switched easing to achieve a specific moment.
fails: When the deviating curve is itself the intended character of that interaction and should persist.

claim: Default to ease-out for UI elements entering or expanding: fast at the start, decelerating into place.
why: Motion that decelerates into rest reads as an object settling, which matches how viewers expect physical panels to behave and makes the arrival feel resolved rather than abrupt.
when: Panels, drawers, sidebars, and other elements moving into view or into an open state.
fails: Exits and dismissals, which usually read better accelerating away (ease-in), and continuous or looping motion, which wants linear timing.

claim: Prototype interactive components to a working state in the design tool before writing any code, so behaviour and timing are settled and reviewable without engineering cost.
why: Interaction quality lives in timing and sequencing that a static mockup cannot communicate; a clickable prototype lets that be judged and corrected while changes are still cheap.
when: Handing off any stateful component — navigation, drawers, menus, toggles — to engineering or to a stakeholder review.
fails: When the interaction depends on real data, physics, or performance characteristics the design tool cannot simulate, where a code prototype is the honest test.

claim: Use a stacked scroll-reveal section when you have three to five sequential items that each need real explanation; below three there is nothing to stack, above five the scroll cost outweighs the payoff.
why: The pattern trades vertical scroll distance for narrative order, so it only pays off when the items are few enough to hold attention and substantial enough to justify a full panel each.
when: Process steps, service tiers, methodology phases — ordered content where each item warrants a paragraph or more.
fails: Long unordered lists, items reducible to a single line, or content users need to scan and compare side by side rather than read in order.

claim: Bind each panel's entrance to a scroll position rather than to a click or tab, so the user's normal downward scroll advances the sequence without a separate interaction.
why: Scroll is the gesture the user is already performing; tying reveal to it makes the order of steps feel like a consequence of reading rather than a control to operate.
when: Sequential content on a marketing or process page where order carries meaning.
fails: Content with no inherent order, or contexts where users need direct access to a specific item without scrolling past the others.

claim: Offer hover-to-expand as the alternative trigger when the same set of panels must be comparable and randomly accessible instead of read in sequence.
why: Hover lets the user jump straight to any panel and back, which suits comparison; scroll enforces an order, which suits narrative.
when: Desktop layouts where the items are peers rather than steps.
fails: Touch devices, where hover has no equivalent and the pattern needs a tap fallback.

claim: Let the incoming panel crop the bottom of the outgoing panel's content rather than aligning panel edges to content edges.
why: A visible cut proves one surface is physically sliding over another, which is what makes the stack read as depth instead of as a list of boxes.
when: Any overlapping-panel or card-stack treatment.
fails: When the clipped region contains information the user still needs — crop decorative overflow and trailing body copy, never the panel's heading, price, or call to action.

claim: Fill each panel with an ordinary two-column layout — supporting media on one side, heading and body on the other — instead of designing a bespoke composition per panel.
why: The motion is already the novel element; a repeated, conventional interior keeps each panel instantly readable and makes the panels legible as members of one series.
when: Multi-panel stacked sections where panels share a role.
fails: Narrow viewports, where the two columns must collapse to a single stacked column.

claim: Wireframe the stack as plain stacked rectangles before designing any panel interior, and treat the interior content as a separate, later decision.
why: The mechanics — panel height, overlap distance, where the stacking starts relative to the section top — are what determine whether the effect works, and they can be judged with empty boxes.
when: Designing any scroll-driven layout effect.

claim: Reject a scroll-driven pattern at the concept stage if it cannot be evaluated in a static frame; prototype it in a tool that plays back real scroll behaviour instead.
why: The value of the pattern lives entirely in the transition, so a static comp will either oversell or undersell it and the decision will be made on the wrong evidence.
when: Any section whose main idea is motion or scroll-linked state.

claim: Start the section with the first panel sitting in a normal, unremarkable page flow, and only begin stacking once the user has scrolled past it.
why: A stretch of ordinary scrolling establishes a baseline, so the moment the second panel starts climbing reads as a deliberate effect rather than a broken layout.
when: Scroll-triggered sections placed mid-page.
fails: Sections placed at the very top of a page, where there is no preceding scroll to establish the baseline.

claim: Treat motion as part of the brand system: pick two or three motion motifs and reuse them at every comparable moment on the site, rather than animating each section differently.
why: A gesture only reads as identity once it repeats; a one-off animation reads as decoration and carries no recognition value.
when: Building a marketing or landing page where the brand needs a distinct feel beyond colour and type.
fails: Not addressed in the chapter; in practice, over-repeating a heavy motif on a long or content-dense page turns signature into friction.

claim: Before animating anything, decide what the focal point should be at that moment in the scroll, and design the motion to move attention from the old focal point to the new one.
why: Motion's job is directing the eye; without a target it just adds visual noise.
when: Any scroll-driven or state-change animation on a page with a clear reading order.

claim: When two stacked sections meet with a hard visual cut, soften the boundary by animating the outgoing section out (translate its elements off-screen and blur its text) while the incoming section slides over the top of it.
why: De-emphasising the old content demotes it to background instead of leaving two competing full-strength layers colliding at the seam.
when: Scroll transitions between full-viewport sections, especially hero to first content block.
fails: Not addressed; blur-out is inappropriate where the outgoing content must stay legible, e.g. sticky nav or persistent data.

claim: Run the same transition in reverse at the bottom of the page so the entry and exit sections mirror each other.
why: Mirrored bookends make the page read as one composed sequence rather than a stack of independent blocks.
when: Pages with a strong hero at the top and a CTA or closing section at the bottom.

claim: Audit the page for stretches with no motion at all; if the top and bottom animate but the middle is static, the middle needs its own smaller motion treatment.
why: Uneven motion distribution makes the unanimated middle read as unfinished or lower-value.
when: Long-scroll landing pages where hero and CTA get the most design attention.

claim: When several items in a set are all equally important and you want each one seen, put them on an automatic timed rotation instead of relying on the user to click through.
why: Passive scrollers won't self-initiate exploration; auto-advance guarantees exposure to every item.
when: A small set (roughly three to five) of equally weighted showcase images or cards.
fails: Not addressed; auto-rotation hurts when items carry dense text, when the user needs to compare items, or when it removes manual control entirely.

claim: Pair automatic movement with a small hover response — a slight scale-up on the image — so the element signals it is interactive.
why: Auto-motion alone can read as a video; a hover response tells the user the item can be engaged with directly.
when: Clickable or explorable media tiles on pointer devices.
fails: Touch-only contexts where hover never fires, so the affordance never appears.

claim: Derive your motion vocabulary by studying a reference site and naming the two or three gestures it repeats, then translating those gestures — not their exact parameters — into your own design.
why: It gives motion a concrete, defensible starting point instead of inventing effects ad hoc per section.
when: Early in a redesign, when establishing the animation direction alongside branding.

claim: Evaluate a motion change by playing the before and after back to back rather than judging the new version alone.
why: Smoothness is only perceptible relative to the cut it replaced; in isolation a transition looks acceptable either way.
when: Reviewing or critiquing scroll and transition work.

claim: Give decorative and illustrative elements an entrance animation instead of leaving them static or applying a default fade-in.
why: A generic fade reads as machine output; a considered entrance reads as authored personality and is the cheapest place to add character, since nothing functional depends on it.
when: Non-critical visual elements — stickers, doodles, illustrations, secondary imagery — enter the viewport on load or scroll.
fails: Applied to elements the user needs immediately (primary nav, form fields, core content), where delayed or animated entry becomes friction.

claim: Choose each element's motion to match what the object is, rather than reusing one shared entrance for every element on the page.
why: Motion that echoes an object's real-world behaviour makes the set feel hand-made and alive; one uniform transition applied everywhere flattens the whole composition back into a template.
when: A layout contains several distinct illustrated or thematic elements — e.g. a balloon should drift in from off-canvas, a star should spin and pop, a card-like object should slide and rotate into place.
fails: In dense interfaces or systematised component libraries where per-element variation breaks consistency and looks chaotic.

claim: Add a small continuous idle motion after an element finishes entering — a slow, low-amplitude drift or bob — for objects that would plausibly keep moving.
why: A fully frozen end state undoes the life the entrance created; a subtle persistent loop keeps the object feeling suspended in a world rather than pasted onto the page.
when: Free-floating illustrated objects with no fixed anchor, like a balloon or floating badge.
fails: Anything the user must read, click, or aim at — perpetual motion on interactive or text elements is distracting and hurts targeting.

claim: Apply easing curves to every entrance and transition rather than shipping linear timing.
why: Real objects accelerate and decelerate; linear interpolation is the single strongest tell that an animation was left at its default settings.
when: Any positional, rotational, or opacity animation.

claim: Use scroll parallax — different scroll speeds for foreground decoration versus the base layout — to create depth instead of building elaborate layered backgrounds.
why: Differential movement is what the eye reads as spatial depth, so it delivers a three-dimensional feel at a fraction of the asset cost.
when: The layout has generous margins or whitespace where decorative elements can travel independently without colliding with content.
fails: Tight, content-dense layouts with no spare space — parallax elements will overlap or obscure text as they drift.

claim: Treat generous margins as an opportunity for motion, not just breathing room: reserve that space for the decorative elements that move.
why: Parallax and drifting entrances need travel distance; whitespace is what makes those movements legible instead of cramped.
when: Deciding layout proportions on a site that intends to use scroll-based motion.

claim: Evaluate motion work by capturing a static 'before' and comparing it directly against the animated 'after'.
why: The gain from motion is only obvious in comparison; judging the animated version alone makes it easy to over- or under-tune.
when: Reviewing whether an animation pass actually improved a screen.

claim: When a page is mostly text, animate the text itself instead of adding decorative imagery — entrance animations plus per-word treatments are what make a copy-heavy page feel designed.
why: Text makes up the overwhelming majority of most sites, so it is where the attention budget actually lives; treating it as static content leaves the page with nothing to hold the eye.
when: Landing pages, hero sections, and portfolios whose primary content is headlines and paragraphs rather than product imagery.
fails: Content-dense reading contexts (docs, articles, dashboards) where animating body copy delays comprehension and irritates repeat visitors.

claim: Judge a text animation by whether it directs attention, not by how technically elaborate it is — prefer the simplest move that makes the eye land where you want.
why: Movement is what captures attention; complexity beyond that point adds cost and load time without adding legibility or focus.
when: Choosing between animation concepts for a headline or hero section.
fails: Cases where the animation is itself the product demo and elaborateness is the point.

claim: Replace a key noun in a headline with a literal visual of the thing it names, animate that visual through its natural behaviour, then transition it out and drop the word into its place.
why: The word gets defined by demonstration rather than assertion, and the swap creates a beat of surprise that anchors the sentence in memory.
when: Headlines containing a concrete, depictable concept — a deadline becoming a filling progress bar, payment becoming falling currency symbols, completion becoming a ticked checkbox.
fails: Abstract nouns with no obvious visual analogue, where the substitution reads as arbitrary decoration and slows the sentence down.

claim: Give each headline line the same entrance treatment (e.g. fade in with a short downward slide) and vary only the word-level flourish after it.
why: A repeated base entrance makes the sequence read as one system, so the differing per-word moments register as intentional accents rather than inconsistency.
when: Multi-line headlines or stacked statements animated in sequence.

claim: Sequence word-level animations along one dominant axis — element rises up and out, replacement drops down into the gap — so the eye follows a continuous path instead of jumping.
why: Motion that shares a direction reads as cause and effect between the outgoing and incoming element, which keeps the swap legible at speed.
when: Any element-to-word or word-to-word replacement inside a line of type.

claim: Close a multi-beat animated sequence with one small punctuating element rather than letting it simply stop.
why: A terminal accent signals the sequence is complete and gives the composition a resting point instead of an ambiguous trailing edge.
when: Choreographed hero sequences with two or more animated lines.

claim: Layer text-level animation on top of existing page-level motion (scroll, transitions) rather than treating them as alternatives — the combination is what reads as a living page.
why: Individually each effect is minor; stacked across scales they produce a continuous sense of responsiveness throughout the visit.
when: Sites already using scroll-driven or page-transition motion.
fails: When both layers fire in the same viewport at the same moment and compete, producing visual noise instead of hierarchy.

claim: On a deliberately minimal, near-text-only site, attach a small hover interaction to nearly every interactive element so simplicity registers as restraint rather than emptiness.
why: Ubiquitous small feedback proves the page is responsive and considered, which is what separates a spare design from an unfinished one.
when: Portfolios and minimal marketing sites with little imagery.
fails: Touch-primary experiences where hover states never fire, leaving the interaction budget unspent.

claim: Reserve a single distinctive effect for one moment on an otherwise plain page instead of distributing effects evenly.
why: A lone effect in a uniform field carries far more weight than the same effect repeated, and gives the page one thing to be remembered for.
when: Text-only portfolios or single-page sites needing one memorable beat.

claim: Rewrite corporate phrasing into concrete, colloquial language — say 'we sweat the details' rather than 'we take pride in our attention to detail'.
why: Plain, physical phrasing reads as a human speaking and is understood instantly; jargon is longer, generic, and interchangeable with every competitor.
when: Marketing copy, headlines, empty states, button labels — anywhere the brand voice is on display.
fails: Regulated, legal, or enterprise-procurement contexts where precise formal terminology is required.

claim: Apply the plain-language standard across the entire site rather than only to the hero, so voice is a system-wide constraint.
why: A friendly headline followed by jargon elsewhere breaks the illusion of a consistent human voice; consistency is what makes the tone a brand asset.
when: Any product or marketing site defining a voice.

claim: Treat motion and copywriting as two levers on the same problem — an animated headline made of stiff language still feels lifeless.
why: Movement earns attention but the words determine what the visitor takes away; polishing one without the other caps the result.
when: Any hero or landing section where a designer is tempted to solve engagement purely with animation.

claim: Build hover and scroll animations natively in the page (CSS/JS or the design tool's own transition system) rather than embedding pre-made third-party animation assets.
why: Imported animations are typically rasterised or scaled video/canvas content, so they render soft against the crisp vector text and UI around them — the mismatch reads as low quality even when viewers can't name the cause.
when: Marketing and product sites where the animation sits inline with sharp typography and UI screenshots.
fails: Genuinely complex 3D or illustrative sequences that cannot be reproduced natively — there, ship at high enough resolution/DPR that it stays sharp on retina displays.

claim: Judge any animation on a marketing page by whether it renders pixel-crisp at 2x device pixel ratio; if it looks soft next to adjacent text, replace or re-export it.
why: Blurriness is the single most visible tell of an imported or under-resolution asset, and it undercuts the perceived quality of the whole page.
when: Reviewing or QA-ing any embedded motion element.

claim: Default to small-scale motion — hover state changes, subtle position or scale shifts, cross-fades between two states — instead of elaborate choreographed sequences.
why: A restrained effect executed cleanly always reads better than an ambitious one executed imperfectly, and the failure mode of ambition is far more visible than the failure mode of restraint.
when: Software/SaaS marketing sites where the content, not the motion, is the product.
fails: Brands whose entire positioning is creative or experiential, where spectacle is the message.

claim: Prototype hover interactions by designing the two end states as separate frames and letting a smart-animate style transition interpolate between them, rather than hand-authoring keyframes.
why: It forces you to think in discrete states, which is exactly how the CSS implementation will work, so the prototype translates directly to build.
when: Designing hover and micro-interaction states in Figma or a similar tool before handoff.
fails: Effects that depend on scroll progress or physics, which state interpolation cannot express.

claim: Use a bento grid — a set of unequal, modular cards tiling a rectangular block — as the default layout for presenting a cluster of related features on one screen.
why: It has become the expected visual language of modern software marketing; sites that ignore it read as dated, and the varied cell sizes let you rank features by importance within a single unified block.
when: A feature or capability section where several items must be shown together and some matter more than others.
fails: Sequential or narrative content where reading order matters, since a bento's varied cell sizes make the scan path ambiguous.

claim: Build the 'simple bento' — plain cards with a heading, short body copy, and a flat icon or minimal graphic — rather than the high-production bento where each cell holds a bespoke 3D render or custom animation.
why: Elaborate bentos require large per-cell production budgets and exist to sell a consumer product; software companies need the layout's structure without that cost, and simpler cells stay legible and easy to update as features change.
when: SaaS and B2B software sites shipping feature overviews on a normal design budget.
fails: Consumer hardware or flagship launch pages where the bento cells are themselves the marketing asset.

claim: Vary the bento's cell sizes and internal layouts across the page rather than repeating one grid configuration, and reuse the pattern in multiple sections at different densities.
why: The bento is a system, not a single component — varying the arrangement keeps repeated use from reading as monotonous while preserving a consistent visual language.
when: Sites that use bento sections more than once.

claim: Every keyboard-triggered action must produce a visible on-screen change; never let a shortcut succeed silently.
