why: Keyboard input gives no inherent visual confirmation the way a click on a button does, so absence of a response reads as failure and the user retries or abandons the command.
when: Any command bound to a key combination in a desktop app, including ones whose real work is instant or happens off-screen.

claim: Prefer an animated transition over an instant swap for shortcut responses; if animation budget is unavailable, at minimum change a discrete visual state (size, position, colour, icon).
why: A transition shows the causal link between the keypress and the result, so the user attributes the change to their own action rather than to the app doing something on its own.
when: Panels, popovers, toolbars, and inline controls that appear, dismiss, or change mode in response to keyboard input.
fails: Ultra-high-frequency commands where the animation would gate the next input; there the transition should be short enough to be interruptible and to not block re-triggering.

claim: Give each outcome of a shortcut flow its own distinct motion: invoke, cancel, and commit should not look alike.
why: Differentiated motion lets the user read the result peripherally without inspecting content — a slide-in reads as 'open', a slide-out as 'discarded', a morph into a confirmation reads as 'saved'.
when: Any keyboard flow with more than one exit path, e.g. a capture panel where Escape discards and Return commits.

claim: Bind panel dismissal to Escape and commit to Return, matching the platform's default keyboard contract.
why: Users carry these bindings across every macOS app; deviating forces relearning and makes a destructive or committing action land on the wrong key.
when: Modal or transient panels, sheets, quick-entry fields, and popovers.
fails: Multi-line text input, where Return must insert a newline and commit needs a modifier such as Command-Return.

claim: Assign a global capture shortcut a three-key combination (e.g. Command-Shift-letter) rather than a two-key one to avoid colliding with the system's reserved bindings.
why: Simple Command-letter combinations are largely spoken for by the OS and by per-app conventions, so a system-wide binding needs an extra modifier to stay unique.
when: Utility apps that register a shortcut that must fire while another app is frontmost.

claim: Let secondary controls sit in a collapsed, reduced-footprint resting state and expand to full size only when invoked by click or shortcut.
why: The tool earns screen space only at the moment of use; keeping it small until then reduces visual noise, and the expansion itself becomes the feedback confirming the invocation.
when: Persistent search fields, command inputs, or utility bars in a dashboard that are used in bursts rather than continuously.
fails: When the control is the app's primary interaction path, or when collapsing hides the app's only discoverable entry point for a task — then the affordance must stay visible.

claim: Make the same action reachable by both pointer and keyboard, and give both paths an identical visual response.
why: The shortcut is an accelerator for a control that still needs to be discoverable by clicking; sharing the response animation keeps the two paths legible as the same command.
when: Any control that has a keyboard accelerator.

claim: After a committed keyboard action, convert the input surface into a transient confirmation (toast) instead of simply closing it.
why: Closing alone is ambiguous — it could mean cancelled or saved; morphing into a confirmation both dismisses the input and reports the result in one continuous gesture.
when: Quick-capture, quick-save, and quick-send flows where the user immediately returns to another app.
fails: Actions the user needs an auditable or persistent record of, where a transient toast disappears before it can be acted on.

claim: Default to small-amplitude, short-duration motion — subtle fades, minor offsets — rather than large, attention-grabbing animation, so the same motion vocabulary can be dropped into any project without redesigning around it.
why: Oversized animation costs render/load performance and demands attention the user did not agree to spend; restrained motion adds polish without either cost.
when: Adding motion to a general-purpose commercial, portfolio, or marketing site where the content, not the animation, is the product.
fails: Sites whose entire premise is spectacle — award-show entries, experimental studio work, game or film promos — where big motion is the content itself.

claim: Classify any animation you are about to build into one of five triggers — page entrance, hover/click, scroll position, continuous loop, or cursor position — and design it against that trigger's constraints rather than as a generic effect.
why: The trigger determines the constraints: entrance runs once and blocks first impression, hover must respond instantly, scroll must track a position, loops run forever and must not fatigue, cursor motion must stay smooth under continuous input.
when: Planning or auditing the motion system for a site, so coverage and consistency across the set can be checked.
fails: Composite effects that fire on more than one trigger (e.g. a scroll-linked loop) do not slot cleanly into a single bucket.

claim: Use a page-entrance animation to cover the load time of heavy first-paint assets — background video, 3D/WebGL scenes, large hero imagery — so the visitor watches an intentional sequence instead of an empty or half-built page.
why: The delay exists regardless; an entrance animation converts unavoidable waiting into designed time and hides the pop-in of assets that arrive late.
when: The first screen depends on assets that cannot render within the first moment of load.
fails: A lightweight page that would otherwise paint instantly — there the entrance adds delay rather than concealing it.

claim: Keep an entrance animation to a single short pass that ends on its own and never repeats within the session, since the viewer sees it before they can act on the page.
why: It occupies the gap between arrival and first interaction; anything longer than the load it covers becomes a toll on every visit.
when: Any load-triggered intro sequence.

claim: Build the simplest entrance that clears the screen: a centred logo on a solid field that fades out to reveal the page is enough — do not add motion complexity to justify the device.
why: A demonstrated minimal fade reads as equally premium as an elaborate sequence, and doubles as a brand impression, at a fraction of the build and performance cost.
when: You want the polish and load-cover benefit of an entrance without an animation budget.

claim: Treat the entrance as free logo real estate — put the wordmark or brand mark in the covering layer so the moment of waiting also delivers brand recall.
why: The overlay already has the viewer's full attention and no competing content; the same seconds can carry identity instead of nothing.
when: Brand-led sites where recognition matters and the identity is not otherwise prominent above the fold.

claim: Verify an entrance animation by hard-refreshing the page rather than by scrubbing a timeline, and evaluate what a first-time visitor actually experiences.
why: Load-triggered motion only exists on load; previewing it in isolation hides its real duration, its interaction with asset timing, and whether it re-fires when it should not.
when: Reviewing or QA-ing any on-load sequence.

claim: Before designing a given animation type, collect two or three shipped sites using that same type — one elaborate, one minimal — and compare what each version buys, so you can choose the cheapest execution that gets the effect.
why: Side-by-side reference exposes which parts of an effect carry the perceived quality and which are decoration you can cut.
when: Building a motion pattern you have not implemented before.

claim: When a preloader overlay exits, animate the underlying page content and background in the same gesture instead of leaving them static — the overlay slides away while the content below moves with a smaller offset in the same direction.
why: A single moving layer over a frozen page reads as a curtain being yanked off a still image; multiple layers moving together read as one continuous piece of motion, so the reveal feels like the page arriving rather than a mask being removed.
when: Any full-screen intro overlay, loading curtain, or page-transition wipe that uncovers content already sitting behind it.
fails: If the underlying content moves as far or as fast as the overlay, the layers lock together and the depth effect collapses; large offsets on body content can also trigger reflow jank or reveal unstyled edges of the layout.

claim: Give the background image or video its own smaller movement during the reveal — a slight drift or scale, distinctly less than the overlay's travel — rather than animating only the foreground text.
why: Differential travel distance between background, content, and overlay produces parallax, which is what supplies the sense of depth and fluidity.
when: Hero sections with a background media layer sitting behind the revealed content.
fails: Not addressed in the chapter.

claim: Keep preloader animations short — target roughly the time it takes to read nothing, on the order of a second or two — and never let the choreography become so intricate that it outlasts the actual load.
why: Users came for the content, not the intro; an interesting animation still registers as a wait once it delays what they asked for.
when: Any preloader or splash animation on a site where content is the point (marketing, portfolio, editorial).
fails: Not addressed in the chapter — though a preloader that ends before assets are ready would just relocate the wait.

claim: Validate a motion detail by building the ablation: rebuild the same transition with that one layer's animation removed and play both back-to-back to confirm the detail is actually earning its complexity.
why: Subtle multi-layer motion is invisible when it works, so the only way to judge whether a layer matters is to compare against its absence.
when: Reviewing or justifying any compound animation where individual contributions are hard to isolate by eye.
fails: Not addressed in the chapter.

claim: Treat an impressive-looking hover effect as a stack of a few simple simultaneous property changes rather than one complex effect, and decompose it into those layers before implementing.
why: Perceived complexity in motion usually comes from several plain transitions firing together, not from any single hard technique.
when: Reverse-engineering or building interactive micro-animations, especially on buttons.
fails: Not addressed in the chapter.

claim: To build a hover button that swaps its label, wrap the button in a container with overflow hidden, stack the outgoing and incoming text so one sits outside the visible box, and translate both upward on hover so one exits as the other enters.
why: The clipping container is what sells the illusion — without it the offscreen label is visible and the motion reads as two elements shuffling rather than one label being replaced.
when: Buttons or nav links where you want a state change that feels mechanical and deliberate rather than a simple colour fade.
fails: If the container clips other required content (focus rings, dropdown menus, tooltips anchored to the button) or if the label wraps to two lines and breaks the fixed translation distance.

claim: Fill a button on hover by animating a small circle: scale it up past the button's bounds while simultaneously reducing its border-radius toward zero, so it lands as a rectangle matching the button shape.
why: Animating scale and radius together turns a background colour change into a directional gesture with a visible origin point, which reads as far more considered than an instant swap.
when: Primary CTAs and hero buttons where a single element earns extra motion detail.
fails: On dense UI with many buttons, where repeating an expensive multi-property animation becomes noisy and costs performance.

claim: Animate the circle's scale and radius rather than the button's own background-color, and keep the circle as a separate absolutely positioned layer behind the label.
why: Transform and radius on a dedicated layer can be composited cheaply and give you control over the fill's origin and direction; a background-color transition can only crossfade uniformly.
when: Any fill-from-a-point button treatment.

claim: Budget effort asymmetrically: accept a multi-layer, labour-heavy build for one or two signature elements, and use the cheap version everywhere else.
why: The build cost is only justified where the element carries enough weight to be looked at; spread thin it produces work without payoff.
when: Deciding which components in a page deserve custom motion.
fails: When deadlines or maintenance burden mean even one bespoke component won't survive later edits.

claim: Before shipping a trendy effect, find a production site in the wild using a restrained version of it, and match their level of restraint rather than the maximal demo version.
why: Real commercial sites have already filtered these effects for whether they still read professional at full scale, so they act as a calibration reference.
when: Adopting an effect you first saw in a design demo or reel.
fails: When the reference site's brand tolerance for playfulness is much higher or lower than the one you're designing for.

claim: Build a scroll-triggered text highlight by filling the text or its container with a two-colour gradient whose stops are positioned nearly on top of each other, producing a hard edge, then animate that edge's position across the element as the user scrolls.
why: Collapsing the gradient's transition zone to near zero turns a soft blend into a crisp wipe line, so a single animatable value (the stop position) drives the whole reveal instead of needing per-character elements.
when: Highlighting or progressively colouring a heading or paragraph as it enters the viewport.
fails: When you need per-word or per-line staggering with independent timing, which a single continuous gradient can't express.

claim: Prefer scroll effects whose implementation cost is low relative to their visual impact when choosing between several candidates.
why: Among effects of similar trendiness, the simplest to build is the one most likely to be maintained and reused correctly.
when: Picking one effect from a shortlist for a real project.

claim: To reveal text on scroll, use the text itself as a mask and animate a filled shape (rectangle or gradient block) across the mask, binding the shape's position to scroll progress rather than to a time-based tween.
why: Masking keeps the reveal glued to the letterforms so the fill appears to sweep through the type, and driving it by scroll position lets the user control the pace, which makes the effect feel responsive instead of played-at-you.
when: Headlines or short statement copy that should reveal as the user scrolls it into view.
fails: Long body paragraphs or copy the user needs immediately — gating readable content behind scroll position hurts scanning and can leave text invisible if scroll never reaches the trigger.

claim: Expose the mask fill's gradient angle as a deliberate choice: a straight (axis-aligned) gradient for a neutral, mechanical sweep, a diagonal one for a more dynamic, hand-drawn feel.
why: The gradient edge is the visible 'wipe' line, so its angle is the main stylistic lever of the whole effect at zero extra implementation cost.
when: Tuning a masked reveal to match a brand's tone once the mechanic already works.

claim: For multi-line reveals, stagger each line's start by a small offset instead of animating all lines simultaneously.
why: Simultaneous reveal reads as one flat block change; staggering creates a reading cadence that guides the eye top-to-bottom through the copy.
when: Headlines wrapping to two or more lines.
fails: Many lines with a large per-line offset — the last line lands so late that the headline feels slow or unfinished on fast scroll.

claim: Before building a scroll effect, audit a site known for dense scroll animation and catalogue several patterns rather than committing to the first one you learn.
why: One technique becomes a crutch and gets applied where it does not fit; a library of options lets the effect be chosen for the content.
when: Starting the motion pass on a marketing or portfolio site.

claim: Keep looping ambient animations simple — one element, one clear trajectory — and reject loops with elaborate or multi-stage choreography.
why: A loop repeats indefinitely in the user's peripheral vision, so any complexity is re-served on every cycle and converts from delight into distraction and then irritation.
when: Decorative motion that runs continuously, unprompted by user action.
fails: One-shot animations triggered by interaction or scroll, where more elaborate choreography is affordable because it plays once.

claim: Slow the playback of looping decorative motion well below the speed you would use for an interaction response, and keep the moving element's travel distance and visual weight small.
why: Fast or large repeating movement competes with content for attention; slow, small motion registers as ambience the eye can ignore.
when: Background or accent loops on a page where reading is the primary task.

claim: Build a simple loop by pairing a curved motion path with a trailing stroke: move an icon along an arc (e.g. a semicircle) while progressively drawing a line along the path behind it.
why: The drawn trail makes an otherwise trivial translation legible as a deliberate gesture and leaves a visible record of the motion, so the effect still reads even when the element is mid-cycle.
when: Small decorative accents around icons, badges, or section markers.

claim: Prefer curved trajectories over straight-line translation for decorative motion.
why: An arc implies momentum and organic movement, whereas linear translation reads as mechanical and draws attention to the fact that it is an animation.
when: Ambient or ornamental motion where the goal is warmth rather than precision.
fails: Functional motion such as menus or drawers, where a direct path better communicates spatial origin.

claim: If a marquee carries readable text, set its scroll speed slow enough that a viewer can finish reading a line before it exits the viewport; only push speed higher when the text is decorative and not meant to be read.
why: A marquee that outruns reading speed converts content into noise — the viewer registers motion but loses the message, so the animation subtracts from the design rather than adding to it.
when: Looping ticker or marquee bands, vertical or horizontal, containing words the user is meant to absorb.
fails: The marquee is pure texture (oversized display type, repeated brand name, abstract fragments), where a faster pass reads as energy rather than lost information.

claim: Use magnetic cursor attraction on the primary CTA: on hover within a small proximity radius, translate the button a fraction of the distance toward the pointer so it appears to meet the cursor.
why: The effect makes the most important interactive target feel eager and easier to hit, concentrating the interaction budget on the one element you want clicked.
when: A single high-priority action — hero CTA, contact button, primary link — on a pointer-driven desktop layout.
fails: Applied to many elements at once, where the constant pulling becomes irritating and dilutes the signal that the magnetic element is the important one.

claim: Budget cursor effects per page: pick one or two elements to carry them and leave the rest static.
why: The effect reads as delightful because it is rare; repeated across a page it becomes friction, since every hover produces motion the user did not ask for.
when: Any desktop site adding pointer-reactive motion.

claim: Never let a cursor-dependent effect carry meaning or affordance on its own — design the tablet and mobile state first, so the element still reads as tappable and important without any hover behaviour.
why: Touch devices have no persistent pointer, so the entire effect disappears; if discoverability or visual interest depended on it, the mobile experience is left with a dead, undifferentiated element.
when: Any hover-driven or pointer-tracking interaction shipped to a responsive site.

claim: Treat cursor-tracking as a reusable mechanic, not a single component: the same pointer-follow logic can drive a custom cursor, a media reveal, or an image that trails the mouse, as long as each instance still obeys the sparing-use and touch-fallback rules.
why: The underlying idea is elements responding to pointer position; once built, that behaviour can be attached to decorative and navigational elements as well as buttons.
when: Sites with an expressive or editorial tone that can absorb stylistic pointer interactions beyond the CTA.
fails: Utility-first interfaces where unexpected pointer-driven movement makes targets harder to hit.

claim: Judge every looping animation by a single test: does it add to the experience, or does it read as flashy and annoying? If it fails, slow it down or cut it rather than tuning it further.
why: Looped motion never stops, so any irritation it causes compounds for the entire time the user is on the page.
when: Evaluating marquees, ambient loops, and other perpetual animation before shipping.

claim: For any pointer-driven effect, design and ship a separate tablet/mobile experience that conveys the same information without hover or cursor position — do not let the effect be the only path to the content.
why: Touch devices have no persistent pointer, so a cursor-tracked reveal simply never fires; anything only reachable through it becomes invisible on those devices.
when: Building hover reveals, cursor-following previews, magnetic elements, or any interaction keyed to mouse coordinates on a responsive site.
fails: Not applicable when the effect is purely decorative and carries no content — there the correct fallback is to drop it entirely rather than rebuild it.

claim: Build a cursor-following element as two separable parts: a listener that stores the current pointer coordinates, and a positioned container that is offset by half its own width and height so its centre — not its top-left corner — sits at those coordinates.
why: Absolutely positioned elements anchor at their top-left by default, so writing raw pointer coordinates to left/top makes the element hang down-right of the cursor instead of surrounding it; the half-size offset is what makes the element feel attached to the pointer.
when: Implementing image previews, tooltips, custom cursors, or hover cards that should appear to be carried by the mouse.
fails: When the follower is large or near a viewport edge — a strictly centred element will overflow offscreen and needs clamping or a flip to the opposite side.

claim: Treat the follow response as an explicit tuning parameter: interpolate the container's position toward the pointer each frame by a factor, and dial that factor up for a tight, immediate snap or down for a heavier, trailing drift.
why: The same mechanism produces very different personalities — a fast follow reads as precise and utilitarian, a slow eased follow reads as fluid and premium — so the character of the interaction is a value you choose rather than a property of the technique.
when: Any element that tracks continuous pointer movement, once the basic positioning works.
fails: Very low follow factors introduce visible lag that reads as jank on interactive targets the user is trying to hit, since the element no longer sits where the pointer is.

claim: Prefer decomposing a trendy effect into its primitives — track a value, position an element, ease the transition — instead of reaching for a plugin or copying a whole implementation.
why: Most of these effects reduce to a handful of simple mechanics, so understanding the primitives makes them cheap to build, adapt, and restyle rather than locked to someone else's markup.
when: Recreating a motion effect seen on an award-winning site with limited engineering time.

claim: Build and verify the static page first, then layer entry animations on top of finished markup rather than animating while the layout is still in flux.
why: Animation code depends on stable element positions and structure; changing layout afterwards invalidates transforms and timing you already tuned.
when: Adding load, reveal, or transition animations to a marketing page or hero section.
fails: Layout itself is animation-driven (e.g. FLIP-based reordering, physics layouts), where structure and motion must be designed together.

claim: Give a loading screen its own top-level sectioning element that is a sibling of the page content, not a child of the header or nav.
why: A full-viewport overlay needs to sit outside the normal document flow and above everything else; nesting it inside a content section couples its stacking and positioning to that section's context.
when: Building a preloader or splash overlay that covers the whole viewport and is later dismissed.
fails: The loader is scoped to a single component or panel, where it should live inside that component's positioned container.

claim: Wrap the loader's contents in a dedicated container element whose only job is grouping, so the group can be centred as one unit.
why: Centring multiple sibling elements individually is fragile; a single wrapper gives one box to centre with flex or absolute positioning, and the children keep their own internal spacing.
when: Any time two or more elements (logo mark plus wordmark, spinner plus label) must sit together in the middle of a region.
fails: There is only one child, where the extra wrapper adds nesting for nothing.

claim: Compose the loader's brand lockup from a separate SVG mark and a live text logotype rather than a single flattened image.
why: Split parts can be animated independently — mark and wordmark can enter on different delays or axes — and the text stays selectable, scalable, and styleable with type rules.
when: The loading screen shows branding that will be animated in or out.
fails: The logotype uses custom lettering or kerning that no available webfont reproduces, in which case the whole lockup should stay vector.

claim: Use a heading element for the loader's wordmark and hang a semantic class on it, keeping the level below the page's real headline.
why: A class-based hook keeps animation and type styling addressable without relying on tag selectors, and reserving the top heading levels for real page content keeps the document outline meaningful when the overlay is removed.
when: Adding decorative or branding text inside an overlay that sits above the real content.
fails: The overlay text is purely ornamental and duplicated elsewhere, where a div or span plus aria-hidden is a cleaner choice.

claim: Layer hero copy over a background image by absolutely positioning the text against the header rather than relying on flow.
why: Decoupling the text from the image's flow lets both be positioned and animated independently over the same area.
when: Full-bleed hero sections where headline text overlays imagery.
fails: Copy length varies enough to overflow the header at small viewports, where flow layout with the image as a CSS background is safer.

claim: For a loading overlay that must cover the whole page, use `position: fixed` with `top: 0; left: 0` and `width: 100vw; height: 100vh` rather than relying on the element's natural block sizing.
why: Fixed positioning removes the overlay from document flow and anchors it to the viewport, so it neither pushes page content around nor scrolls away; the explicit offsets kill any inherited margin or gap at the edges, and the viewport units guarantee it spans the full screen regardless of how much content sits behind it.
when: Building a preloader, splash screen, or any blocking full-screen layer that sits over an entire page.
fails: On mobile browsers where `100vh` overshoots because of collapsing address bars — prefer `100dvh` or `inset: 0` there; also wrong for overlays scoped to a single card or section, which should use `position: absolute` inside a positioned parent.

claim: Set `z-index` on an overlay at the moment you make it positioned, not after you notice something bleeding through.
why: Stacking bugs surface late and are read as visual glitches rather than CSS ordering problems; deciding the layer up front while you already have the element's role in mind is cheaper than debugging it once the page has more layers.
when: Any time you write `position: fixed` or `absolute` on an element whose whole job is to sit above other content.
fails: When the overlay is nested inside an ancestor that creates its own stacking context (a transformed, filtered, or opacity-reduced parent) — a high z-index there still cannot escape the parent's layer.

claim: Give a blocking overlay an opaque background colour so nothing underneath shows through while the load state is active.
why: The overlay's purpose is to conceal an unfinished page; a transparent or partial background lets half-rendered layout and unloaded assets flash into view and undercuts the illusion of a polished load.
when: Preloaders and splash screens that hide the page until assets or animations are ready.
fails: For modal-style overlays where the underlying context should stay legible — those want a translucent scrim instead.

claim: Make the overlay itself a flex container so the loader graphic can be centred by the parent rather than by margin or transform hacks on the child.
why: A viewport-sized flex parent gives you both axes of centring from one place, which keeps the child free of positioning rules and lets it be swapped or resized without touching its alignment.
when: Centring a single loader element — spinner, counter, logo — inside a full-screen container.
fails: If the child is later animated with transforms, translate-based centring on the child would fight the flex alignment; keep centring entirely on the parent in that case.

claim: Add new component CSS as a fresh block appended below existing rules instead of interleaving it into current selectors.
why: Keeping a feature's styles contiguous makes the overlay easy to read, move, or delete as a unit, and avoids accidentally disturbing rules that already work.
when: Layering a self-contained UI feature onto an existing stylesheet during a build.
fails: In a stylesheet where cascade order carries meaning — appending can silently override earlier rules of equal specificity.

claim: Save and check the browser as soon as the container has dimensions and a background, before adding any child styling or animation.
why: A full-screen block of solid colour is an unambiguous visual signal that positioning, sizing, and layering are all correct; confirming the shell first means any later bug belongs to the contents, not the container.
when: Building up a layout element property by property.

claim: Size a preloader logo as a percentage of the viewport (start around 10% width) instead of a fixed pixel value, then eyeball and adjust.
why: A relative width keeps the mark proportionate across screen sizes, and the exact figure is a visual judgement best made by trying a value and looking at it.
when: Sizing a single hero mark or logo that must feel the same weight on any screen during a full-viewport load screen.
fails: Very small or very large viewports, where a pure percentage can render the mark illegibly small or overwhelmingly large without a clamp or min/max bound.

claim: When a flex child looks off-centre, check the container's width before touching the child's margins — a full-width container with default start alignment will park content on the left even though nothing is 'wrong' with the child.
why: Flex containers default to packing items at the main-axis start; extra container width becomes trailing empty space that reads as a leftward offset.
when: Debugging visual misalignment of a single item inside a flex wrapper that spans more space than its contents.
fails: The offset comes from something else — asymmetric padding, an absolutely positioned ancestor, or transform origin — in which case main-axis alignment won't fix it.

claim: Centre a lone element inside its flex container by setting both main-axis and cross-axis alignment to centre on the parent, rather than adding auto margins or offsets to the child.
why: Alignment on the parent keeps the child free of layout-specific overrides, so the same child can be reused or animated without inherited positioning baggage.
when: A flex container holds one or a few items that should sit dead centre both ways.
fails: Multiple children need distinct alignments, or the container's size is itself content-driven so there is no slack to distribute.

claim: Set the animated element's starting opacity to 0 in CSS before writing any animation code, so the intro animation has a defined invisible origin.
why: Without a hidden start state the element flashes fully visible during page load and before the script runs, breaking the reveal.
when: Any JS-driven entrance animation where the element must not be seen until the timeline plays it in.
fails: JavaScript is disabled or the animation library fails to load — the element then stays permanently invisible unless a no-JS fallback restores it.

claim: Create the animation timeline in a paused state and hold it in a named constant, instead of letting it autoplay on creation.
why: A paused timeline separates authoring the sequence from triggering it, so playback can be deferred until assets are ready or another event fires, and the handle allows later control.
when: Building a preloader or entrance sequence whose start must be coordinated with load events or other timelines.
fails: Simple decorative animations that should just run on paint — pausing adds a trigger you must remember to fire, and forgetting it leaves the UI stuck in its hidden start state.

claim: Build the CSS resting/hidden state first and only then move to the animation script.
why: The animation only interpolates between states, so the layout and starting values must be settled before motion code is meaningful.
when: Any workflow combining static styling with a JS animation library.

claim: Build a preloader as a single named timeline with sequentially labelled steps rather than separate independent animations, so ordering and re-timing stay in one place.
why: A timeline enforces sequence automatically; independent tweens each need hand-managed delays that drift out of sync when any duration changes.
when: Any multi-step entrance/exit sequence where step B must reliably follow step A.
fails: Steps that are genuinely independent and should overlap freely, or one-off hover/interaction states where timeline overhead adds nothing.

claim: Once a timeline is declared, chain subsequent steps by referencing the same timeline object instead of re-instantiating it per step.
why: Re-declaring creates a second, unsynchronised timeline, which breaks the sequencing the pattern exists to provide.
when: Adding the second and later steps to any JS animation timeline.

claim: Insert a hold of roughly 1 second before revealing the brand mark, so the logo lands as a deliberate beat rather than appearing in the same instant as everything else.
why: A short pause gives the eye a settling point and makes the reveal feel authored and premium instead of accidental.
when: Brand-forward preloaders where the logo is the focal moment.
fails: Fast-loading pages or repeat visits, where an enforced delay makes the site feel artificially slow — gate or skip it after first load.

claim: Animate the logo from hidden to opacity 1 as an explicit tween rather than leaving it visible by default, so its arrival is a controlled moment in the sequence.
why: Elements that are already visible at frame zero cannot participate in the choreography; starting hidden hands timing control to the timeline.
when: Any element whose entrance is part of a scripted load sequence.
fails: Content that must remain visible if JS fails to run — guard with a no-JS fallback so the page isn't permanently blank.

claim: Dismiss a full-screen preloader by translating it out of the viewport (e.g. -100% on the Y axis) rather than fading it out or toggling display.
why: A directional slide reads as a physical curtain lifting and reveals the underlying page progressively; a fade or hard hide gives no sense of transition between states.
when: Full-bleed overlay panels covering the page during load.
fails: Overlays that are not full-bleed, where sliding exposes the page edge awkwardly; also avoid if the overlay isn't removed from the flow afterwards, since an off-screen fixed panel can still trap pointer events or extend scroll.

claim: Express the overlay's exit translation as a percentage of the element's own height (-100%) instead of a pixel value.
why: A percentage adapts to any viewport height, guaranteeing the panel clears the screen exactly on mobile and desktop without recalculating on resize.
when: Moving full-viewport elements fully in or out of frame.
fails: Elements sized independently of the viewport, where a percentage of self-height may under- or over-shoot the intended distance.

claim: Keep individual preloader steps around 1 second and preview each one immediately after writing it before moving to the next.
why: Timing is judged by eye, not by number; checking each beat in isolation prevents compounding a misjudged duration through the rest of the sequence.
when: Authoring motion incrementally in code.
fails: Total sequence length matters — several 1s beats stacked serially can push a preloader past the point users tolerate.

claim: Pick the animation's easing curve from the same curve used in the design mockup rather than accepting the library default, so the built animation reads as the same motion the designer approved.
why: Duration and distance can be matched exactly and the animation will still feel wrong if the acceleration profile differs; easing is what carries the perceived character of a motion.
when: Translating a motion prototype from a design tool into code, where the designer specified a custom bezier.

claim: For premium-feeling entrance animations, use an exponential ease-in-out over roughly 1.2-1.4 seconds: a long, unhurried curve that starts and ends nearly still with a fast middle.
why: The extreme acceleration profile makes the element feel like it settles into place rather than stopping abruptly, and the longer duration gives the eye time to register the arrival as deliberate.
when: Hero or above-the-fold reveal animations on a loading sequence, where the motion is the first impression and nothing is blocking the user.
fails: Interaction feedback — button presses, hover states, menu toggles — where anything past ~300ms reads as lag rather than polish.

claim: Compose a reveal from two stacked properties rather than one: fade opacity in first, then translate the element upward into position.
why: A pure slide reads as mechanical and a pure fade reads as flat; overlapping the two gives the element a sense of arriving from somewhere.
when: Text or content blocks entering on page load.

claim: Stagger a load sequence so chrome (navigation, header) resolves after the primary content has finished moving, instead of animating everything at once.
why: Simultaneous entrances give the eye no order to follow; deferring secondary UI creates a clear reading path and lets the hero own the first moment.
when: Multi-element page-load choreography where one element is clearly the focal point.

claim: Before animating any element, explicitly set its hidden start state — opacity zero, offset position — as a separate instantaneous step, not as part of the tween.
why: Without a declared start state the element renders visible for the first frames and then jumps, which is more noticeable than no animation at all.
when: Any element whose animation begins after page paint, especially one delayed to the end of a sequence.

claim: Choose one home for initial hidden states — either the stylesheet or an instant JS set call — and apply it consistently across the sequence rather than mixing per element.
why: Splitting start states across two systems means debugging a flash requires checking both; a single source keeps the sequence's starting conditions readable in one place.
when: Any JS-driven load animation with several elements that start hidden.
fails: The two approaches genuinely differ in consequence — CSS-authored hidden states persist if JS fails to load, leaving content permanently invisible, which argues for CSS only when paired with a no-JS fallback.

claim: Reload and watch the animation at full speed after each timing change instead of reasoning about the numbers.
why: Easing and duration values are not legible as text; the only reliable check on whether a curve feels right is seeing it play.
when: Iterating on motion parameters.

claim: To reveal text with a slide-up, pre-position it with a percentage-based Y transform equal to 100% (its own height), then tween that value back to 0.
why: Offsetting by exactly one element-height parks the text just outside its own clipping container, so the return tween reads as the text rising into an empty frame rather than sliding in from an arbitrary distance.
when: Revealing a headline, word, or line that sits inside a wrapper you can clip with overflow hidden.
fails: The wrapper is taller than the text (extra padding or line-height) — then 100% overshoots and leaves dead time before the glyphs appear; measure or tighten the wrapper first.

claim: Use percentage-based transform units rather than pixels or viewport units for slide reveals, because the percentage is measured against the animated element's own dimensions.
why: The offset then scales automatically with font size, line count, and breakpoint, so the same code produces the same visual reveal on every screen without recalculating distances.
when: Any enter/exit transform whose correct distance is 'exactly one element out of view'.
fails: You actually want the element to travel a screen-relative distance (a full-viewport panel wipe) — use viewport units there instead.

claim: Animate a text reveal on a separate wrapper element from the one being clipped or moved, so the two transforms don't fight.
why: A single element can only hold one transform state; splitting the mask/clip from the moving content lets you offset and restore the inner layer independently of the outer layer's own motion.
when: Building masked type reveals, split-line headings, or any reveal where a container also animates.

claim: Give paired elements in the same transition the identical duration and easing curve — here 1.3s with an exponential in-out — rather than tuning each one separately.
why: Matching the curve makes the two moving layers read as one physical gesture; differing eases make them look like two unrelated animations that happen to overlap.
when: Two or more elements move together as part of a single perceived transition, such as a loader exiting while content enters.
fails: You deliberately want a lead/follow or staggered relationship, where a slight offset in timing (not easing) creates hierarchy.

claim: Overlap the incoming content's reveal with the outgoing loader's exit using a negative timeline position offset instead of letting the tweens run back to back.
why: Sequential playback makes the total transition feel twice as long and produces a dead beat where nothing is on screen; overlapping keeps continuous motion and cuts perceived load time.
when: Chaining an exit animation into an entrance on the same timeline.
fails: Overlapping so much that the loader is still covering the text as it moves — the reveal is then wasted behind the mask.

claim: Use exponential in-out easing for full-screen loader transitions rather than linear or a gentle ease.
why: Expo in-out starts slow, covers most of the distance very fast, and settles softly, which lets a long travel distance complete quickly without feeling abrupt — the signature of a 'premium' feeling transition.
when: Large elements travelling long distances, such as a full-viewport overlay leaving the screen.
fails: Small UI movements like button hovers, where the aggressive middle section reads as a glitch.

claim: When two elements in a load sequence belong to the same visual moment, start them at the same timestamp with the timeline's position parameter rather than letting them queue back-to-back.
why: A timeline defaults to strict sequencing, which stretches a single perceived gesture into two separate events and makes the intro feel longer and choppier than intended.
when: Building a multi-step entrance timeline where certain elements read as one composite reveal (e.g. a heading and its underline, or a mask and the content behind it).
fails: Overlapping steps that are meant to be read in order — if the viewer needs to register element A before B, concurrency destroys the narrative and everything lands as visual noise.

claim: Author every step of a load animation on a single timeline and control ordering through relative offsets, instead of hand-tuning delays on independent tweens.
why: Offsets stay correct when earlier durations change; hardcoded delays silently drift out of sync the moment any upstream timing is edited.
when: Any sequence with more than two or three choreographed steps.
fails: Animations triggered by unrelated, unpredictable user events, which have no shared origin point to offset from.

claim: Fade supporting chrome such as the navigation bar in as the final beat of the load sequence, after the hero content has resolved.
why: Ordering the reveal from primary content outward tells the viewer where to look first; chrome arriving last reads as the interface settling into place around the message.
when: Premium landing-page or hero intros where a persistent nav sits above content that is itself animating in.
fails: The nav is the interaction the user came for (e.g. a returning-user dashboard), where delaying it just delays their task.

claim: Keep terminal opacity fades short — roughly 0.3s — rather than matching the longer durations used by the sequence's headline moves.
why: The final element only needs to appear, not perform; a long fade on a trailing item leaves the page feeling unfinished after the main animation has already paid off.
when: Closing out an entrance sequence with secondary UI that fades from 0 to full opacity.
fails: The element is the focal reveal, or it is also travelling a large distance, in which case a longer, eased duration is warranted.

claim: Skip a custom easing curve on pure opacity tweens this short and let the default handle it.
why: Easing communicates physical momentum, which only becomes perceptible on transforms or over longer durations; on a 0.3s fade the difference between curves is below the threshold of notice, so specifying one is unearned complexity.
when: Short fades where no position, scale, or rotation is changing.
fails: Fades running long enough to perceive their curve, or opacity changes paired with movement — those need an ease so the two properties agree.

claim: Reload and watch the full sequence in the browser after each timing change rather than reasoning about the numbers.
why: Whether an overlap reads as one gesture or two is a perceptual judgement that duration values on their own cannot predict.
when: Any iteration on animation choreography.

claim: Give a floating loader container a translucent background rather than an opaque one — append an 8-digit hex alpha (e.g. `#RRGGBB61`, roughly 38%) instead of using a solid fill.
why: A semi-transparent surface lets the underlying page show through, so the loader reads as a layer floating above the composition rather than a hard-edged box cut out of it.
when: Styling a pill, badge, or overlay container that sits on top of other content during a load or transition state.
fails: Over content with insufficient contrast — a translucent fill can drop the container's text below accessible contrast, in which case use a solid fill or add a backdrop blur.

claim: To make an element fully pill-shaped, set `border-radius` to a value far larger than half its height (e.g. 100px) rather than computing the exact half-height.
why: Border-radius clamps at half the shorter dimension, so an oversized value produces a perfect semicircular cap at any height and stays correct if the element's size changes.
when: Any capsule/pill-shaped container whose height is dynamic or not yet finalised.
fails: On large rectangular surfaces (cards, modals) where an oversized radius rounds far more than intended — there you want an explicit small radius.

claim: Pad pill-shaped containers asymmetrically — roughly 3x more horizontal than vertical padding (e.g. 10px top/bottom, 30px left/right).
why: The rounded end caps eat into usable horizontal space, so equal padding visually crowds the content against the curves; extra side padding restores optical balance and keeps the pill's proportions elongated.
when: Pills, chips, badges, and buttons with a fully rounded radius.

claim: Set an element's animate-in properties to their starting values in CSS (e.g. `opacity: 0`) before writing any animation code, and confirm the element is correctly hidden in the browser.
why: Declaring the from-state in CSS prevents a flash of the un-animated element on first paint, and verifying it visually catches selector or specificity mistakes before JS timing bugs can mask them.
when: Building any entrance animation where the element should not be visible until its cue.
fails: If the JS that animates it fails to run or errors, the element stays permanently invisible — guard with a fallback or a JS-enabled class.

claim: Build the full static appearance of every animated element first, then write the animation code as a separate pass.
why: Animation is a change between two known states; if the end state isn't nailed down visually, you end up debugging layout and timing simultaneously.
when: Multi-element load sequences and any scripted entrance animation.

claim: When an animation needs a dimension the CSS doesn't declare (such as the height of a content-sized element), read it from the rendered DOM in JS and derive the other dimension from it rather than hardcoding a number.
why: Content-sized elements change height with font, text length, and viewport; a measured value keeps a derived property such as a circular collapse width correct across all of them.
when: Animating between a content-sized pill and a fixed-ratio shape (e.g. collapsing a pill to a circle, where width must equal height).
fails: Measuring before fonts/images load or while the element is display:none returns a wrong or zero value — measure after layout settles and with the element rendered.

claim: When an animation depends on an element's real size or position, read that value from the DOM at runtime instead of hardcoding a number into the animation.
why: Rendered dimensions shift with viewport, font loading, and content length; a hardcoded value silently desyncs the animation from what the user sees.
when: Any transform whose distance, height, or offset must line up with a real layout element — a nav collapsing, a panel sliding to the height of its content, an element travelling to another element's edge.
fails: The measurement is taken before layout settles (fonts still loading, images unsized, element hidden with display:none) — you get zero or a stale value and the animation lands wrong.

claim: Immediately log any measured layout value and confirm both the number and its unit before building animation logic on top of it.
why: Measurement APIs vary in what they return — bare numbers, px strings, computed vs. inline values — and a wrong-typed value produces an animation that runs without error but moves the wrong distance.
when: The first time you introduce any runtime measurement into an animation sequence.
fails: Left in shipped code; the check is a build-time step, not a runtime feature.

claim: Create animation timelines in a paused state by default, then trigger playback explicitly from your own control flow.
why: Load and reveal sequences must fire in a deliberate order tied to readiness signals; a timeline that autoplays on creation runs before its dependencies (measurements, asset loads, prior beats) are settled.
when: Any multi-step load, reveal, or transition sequence where several timelines must be coordinated.
fails: A standalone decorative loop with no ordering dependency — pausing just adds a trigger you have to remember to call.

claim: Reuse one animation library and one construction pattern across every sequence in a build rather than mixing approaches per element.
why: A shared pattern makes timelines composable — they can be nested, sequenced, and timed against each other — and removes the cost of context-switching between mental models mid-build.
when: A project with several coordinated animated sequences, especially a multi-part load or intro.

claim: Split animation work into a measurement phase and a movement phase, and treat the measurement phase as where the real difficulty sits.
why: Once the correct value is in a variable, the tween itself is a one-line declaration; most animation bugs trace back to a wrong or mistimed measurement rather than to the easing or duration.
when: Building any layout-dependent motion where the distance is not a fixed design constant.
fails: Choreography-heavy sequences where the timing and easing genuinely carry the complexity, not the numbers.

claim: Name measurement constants after the element and property they describe so the value's origin is readable at the call site.
why: A tween referencing a descriptive constant self-documents what the number represents, which matters when the same timeline juggles several measured offsets.
when: Storing runtime-measured layout values for later use in a timeline.

claim: When an element must animate out of a state it never naturally occupies (scale 0, zero width, off-canvas), use a two-state tween that declares both start and end values rather than an end-only tween that inherits whatever the browser computed.
why: An end-only tween reads the current rendered state as its starting point, so the animation is at the mercy of CSS defaults; declaring the start explicitly makes the motion deterministic and self-documenting.
when: Entrance and reveal animations where the initial state is a deliberate, non-default value.
fails: For exit animations or state changes that should begin from wherever the element currently is — forcing a start value there causes a visible snap before the tween runs.

claim: Animate a nav container in from scale 0 to scale 1 over roughly 0.8s as the first beat of the reveal.
why: Scaling from nothing gives the element a single point of origin, so it reads as emerging rather than fading in place; sub-second timing keeps the load sequence from feeling slow.
when: Premium/branded loading sequences where the nav is meant to arrive as a distinct event rather than just being present.

claim: Split a compound reveal into separate tweens per property — scale first, then max-width — instead of animating everything in one tween.
why: Separate tweens let each property carry its own duration and position on the timeline, so the element can pop into existence and then expand as two readable stages rather than one blurred simultaneous change.
when: Reveals where the element both appears and changes size or shape.
fails: When the two properties are meant to read as one gesture — splitting them then makes the motion feel mechanical and stepped.

claim: Set the element's authored CSS to its collapsed value (max-width: 0) before animating it open; the stylesheet must own the resting state, not the animation library.
why: The animation only expands from whatever the CSS declares; if the stylesheet still holds the full open width, the tween has nothing to reveal and the element flashes fully formed on load.
when: Any width/height/max-dimension reveal driven by a JS timeline.
fails: If the collapsed state is set only in CSS with no JS fallback, the content is inaccessible when scripts fail to load — the collapsed state needs a no-JS escape.

claim: Use max-width rather than width when animating a container open, so the element's intrinsic content still governs its final size.
why: Clamping the maximum lets the layout resolve the natural width, so the same animation works across varying content lengths and breakpoints without hardcoded end values.
when: Expanding containers whose contents are of unknown or responsive width.
fails: Elements with no intrinsic width to fall back on, where max-width alone produces no visible expansion.

claim: Name each segment of a load timeline (nav, hero, etc.) as you build it, and append segments in the order they should play.
why: A named, sequential timeline makes the choreography editable — you can retime or reorder a stage later without unpicking the whole animation.
when: Multi-element load sequences built as a single timeline.

claim: When morphing an element between two shapes, animate from an explicitly zeroed starting dimension rather than letting the element inherit its natural size — set the property to 0 first, then tween from that.
why: A tween has no reliable starting point if the element's computed size is whatever the layout gives it; zeroing the property makes the animation's origin deterministic.
when: Animating width/height/max-width on an element whose resting size comes from content or layout rules.

claim: To make an element read as a circle at the start of a shape-morph, set its constrained dimension equal to the same token that drives its other dimension (e.g. max-width = the nav-height variable), and pair that with a full border-radius.
why: A circle is just equal width and height; sourcing both from one variable guarantees they stay equal even if the value changes later.
when: Building a shape that expands from a dot or pill into a panel.
fails: If the two dimensions are set from separate hardcoded numbers, they drift out of sync when one is edited and the shape stops being round.

claim: Drive paired dimensions from a single named variable rather than repeating a literal value, so the shape relationship survives future edits.
why: The equality between the two dimensions is the design intent; a variable encodes that intent, duplicated numbers only coincidentally satisfy it.
when: Any CSS/JS animation where two properties must remain equal or proportional.

claim: Give a large-travel shape expansion roughly 1.2–1.4 seconds — long enough to be read as a deliberate transformation rather than a snap.
why: The element is covering a lot of distance and changing shape category; too short and the morph is illegible, too long and it stalls the user.
when: Hero-scale or full-screen menu reveals where the animation is the moment, not a micro-interaction.
fails: Small UI feedback (button states, hovers) at this duration feels sluggish and unresponsive.

claim: Use an expo ease-in-out for premium-feeling expansion animations: a slow, weighted start, a fast middle, and a long deceleration into rest.
why: The extreme acceleration curve makes the element feel physically heavy and intentional, which is what separates a 'premium' motion from a default linear or generic ease.
when: Large elements travelling a long distance, especially overlays and page transitions.
fails: Rapid, repeated, or interruptible interactions, where the slow tail makes the UI feel unresponsive.

claim: Sequence a menu reveal as container-first, contents-second: finish or nearly finish the shape expansion before bringing the links in.
why: Content fading in while its container is still resizing competes for attention and looks like two unrelated animations happening at once.
when: Any overlay, modal, or drawer that contains its own list of items.

claim: When several sibling elements need the same entrance animation, select them as one collection and animate the group with a stagger instead of writing a separate tween per element.
why: Per-element tweens are verbose, hard to retime, and break when the number of items changes; a grouped selection scales automatically and gives you rhythm control from one parameter.
when: Nav links, list items, cards, or any repeated set that should appear in sequence.
fails: Items that need genuinely different animations or different targets still warrant individual tweens.

claim: Animate list-item entrances with opacity as the base property, layering other transforms on top rather than replacing it.
why: Opacity is cheap to composite and reads as 'arriving' without shifting layout.
when: Revealing text links inside an already-positioned container.

claim: When several sibling elements share the same entrance animation, pass them as an array of targets to one tween rather than writing a separate tween per element.
why: One tween keeps the timing logic in a single place, so changing the duration or easing updates the whole group at once and the code stays readable as the group grows.
when: Multiple elements in the same region (nav items, logo, CTA button) animate with identical properties and only differ in start time.
fails: Elements need genuinely different properties, easings, or non-linear ordering — then separate tweens or nested timelines are clearer.

claim: Use a stagger value to offset the start of each element in a group instead of manually computing per-element delays.
why: The animation engine derives each element's offset from one number, so the cascade stays consistent and re-orders automatically if you add or remove an element.
when: A group of elements should enter in sequence in DOM order.
fails: You need a custom entrance order that does not match DOM order, or per-element delays that are not evenly spaced.

claim: For a header/nav reveal, set the stagger offset to roughly one third of the item duration — e.g. 0.2s stagger against a 0.6s duration.
why: An offset shorter than the duration means the items overlap in flight, so the group reads as one continuous cascade rather than a series of discrete, plodding steps; a stagger equal to or larger than the duration makes each item finish before the next begins and the sequence feels slow.
when: Three to five elements revealing as part of a page load or header entrance.
fails: With a long list (10+ items) the same stagger accumulates into an unacceptably long total; scale the stagger down or use a distributed stagger so the total stays bounded.

claim: Keep a load-in animation's per-element duration around 0.6s so a three-item cascade completes in roughly one second total.
why: The whole entrance has to finish before the user starts interacting; total time is duration plus stagger times the item count, so per-item duration is the main lever on perceived page-load speed.
when: Premium page-load sequences where polish matters but the user must reach a usable interface quickly.
fails: Ambient or looping decorative motion, where longer durations are appropriate.

claim: Animate reveals toward the visible state (opacity to 1) and rely on CSS for the hidden starting state, rather than animating from visible to hidden and back.
why: Declaring the hidden state in CSS means elements never flash at full opacity before the script runs, and the tween only has to describe the destination.
when: Entrance animations that run once on page load.
fails: If JS fails or is blocked, CSS-hidden content stays invisible — provide a no-JS fallback for anything essential.

claim: Build the entrance as a paused timeline and explicitly call play() at the point you want it to start, rather than letting tweens auto-run on creation.
why: Separating construction from playback lets you gate the reveal behind a real readiness signal — fonts loaded, preloader finished, assets decoded — instead of firing while the page is still settling.
when: Load animations that must be sequenced after a preloader or asset-ready event.
fails: Simple always-on animations with no readiness dependency, where an explicit play call is unnecessary ceremony.

claim: Build a wipe/reveal effect as a single absolutely-positioned child inside the element it covers: set position:absolute, top:0, left:0, width:100%, height:100%, and give the parent a positioning context — then animate one dimension rather than the text itself.
why: Animating an overlay's geometry leaves the underlying text untouched, so glyph rendering, wrapping and layout stay stable while the reveal plays; the overlay also inherits its target's exact bounds for free.
when: Any wipe, sweep, curtain or masked-reveal of a text run or small UI block during a load or entrance sequence.
fails: The parent has no position other than static (the wipe escapes to the nearest positioned ancestor or the viewport), or the content reflows mid-animation so the 100%/100% box no longer matches what it is meant to cover.

claim: Set the overlay's animated dimension to its full 100% resting value first, get it visually correct, and only then convert that property into the keyframe/transition handle.
why: Starting from the covered end-state makes the overlay's alignment and colour verifiable statically, before motion hides mistakes; you then animate a value you have already confirmed is right.
when: Authoring any transform- or size-driven reveal where the static covered state and the animated state differ.

claim: Treat animation timing values as tuning parameters, not fixed correct numbers — ship a rough pass, view it at real speed, then adjust durations and delays by eye.
why: Perceived pacing of a loader depends on the whole sequence and on the content behind it; the number that reads well is found by watching, not by calculating.
when: Multi-step load and entrance sequences where several elements animate in relation to each other.
fails: Endless eyeballing without a fixed total budget — a loader still has to clear within the time the real asset load allows.

claim: Reload and watch each animation variant end-to-end before starting the next one.
why: Load animations only exist in time; a variant that looks right in the editor can stutter, overlap or land at the wrong moment, and catching that before the next variant is built keeps the fault isolated.
when: Building a set of sibling animation variants in one pass.

claim: Keep every variant in a family on the same markup skeleton — one screen container plus one text element — and let CSS alone create the difference between variants.
why: A shared structure means each new variant costs almost no HTML, variants stay swappable at runtime, and the differences live in one reviewable place.
when: Producing a library of interchangeable loading or transition treatments for the same project.
fails: A variant genuinely needs different DOM (e.g. per-character or per-line splitting), where forcing the shared skeleton adds more hacks than it saves.

claim: Give animation-only elements a name that states their behaviour rather than their appearance — e.g. a class describing the wipe, not the colour or position.
why: The visual properties of these layers change during tuning; the role they play in the sequence does not, so behaviour-named hooks survive restyling.
when: Naming non-semantic overlay and mask elements added purely for motion.

claim: When adding a new element that mirrors one you already styled, duplicate the existing rule block and edit the two or three values that differ instead of authoring fresh CSS.
why: The sibling element already encodes correct positioning, stacking, and box behaviour; copying keeps the pieces visually consistent and cuts the number of decisions down to the ones that actually vary.
when: Building repeated layers in the same composition — stacked text lines, paired image panels, multiple masked reveals.
fails: The two elements differ structurally rather than cosmetically; copied rules then carry hidden assumptions (a positioning context or overflow rule) that silently break the new element.

claim: Size hero/background media in percentages of its container rather than fixed pixels, so the element scales with the stage instead of needing a rewrite per breakpoint.
why: Percentage sizing binds the element to the composition it sits inside, so one number controls its proportion at any viewport size.
when: Full-bleed or near-full-bleed media inside a sized wrapper in a load or transition animation.
fails: The parent has no resolved height — percentage height then collapses to zero or resolves against the wrong ancestor.

claim: When you shrink an absolutely positioned element's height, add an equal offset to its top so the visible band stays centred; e.g. height 80% pairs with top 10%.
why: Reducing height alone removes space from one edge only, so the element drifts off-centre and content crops at the opposite edge; splitting the removed 20% evenly as a 10% top offset restores the intended centring.
when: Absolutely positioned layers whose height you tune by percentage inside a positioned parent.
fails: The element is already centred by transform, flex, or inset-based centring — adding a manual top offset then double-shifts it.

claim: Set an animating element's start state in CSS — opacity 0 and width 0% for a wipe-in — rather than relying on the animation library to set it at runtime.
why: If the initial state lives only in JS, the element flashes at full size in the gap between first paint and script execution, which is exactly the moment a load animation is meant to cover.
when: Any element that should be invisible or unrevealed at frame zero of a load or intro animation.
fails: The element must remain visible and usable when JS fails to load — hiding it in CSS makes the no-JS state permanently blank.

claim: Animate a text reveal by growing width from 0% while its container clips overflow, instead of fading or sliding the text.
why: A width tween on a clipping wrapper produces a hard wipe edge that uncovers the glyphs progressively, which reads as more deliberate and premium than a uniform fade.
when: Headline or large display type in an intro sequence where you want a directional reveal.
fails: The text wraps or reflows as width changes — the wipe then rewraps lines mid-animation instead of uncovering fixed glyphs; requires nowrap and a fixed intrinsic width.

claim: Create the timeline paused, then append tweens to it, and trigger playback explicitly rather than letting it autoplay on construction.
why: A paused timeline separates authoring the choreography from deciding when it runs, so playback can be gated on asset loading, scroll position, or a user action instead of firing at an arbitrary point during page setup.
when: Load animations, scroll-triggered sequences, and any timeline whose start depends on an external condition.
fails: Nothing ever calls play — the sequence silently never runs and the pre-hidden CSS start state leaves the UI blank.

claim: Group a multi-step reveal into one named timeline rather than scattering independent tweens, naming it for the effect it produces (e.g. a `wipe` timeline).
why: A single timeline gives one handle for sequencing, delays, reversal, and scrubbing, and the name documents intent at the call site.
when: Any animation with more than one moving part that must stay in sync.

claim: Judge size and position by rendering and looking at the result, adjusting values in small passes, instead of calculating them up front.
why: Composition problems like 'too big' or 'cropped at the bottom' only surface visually; two quick render-and-tweak cycles resolve them faster than deriving the numbers.
when: Tuning layout of visual media in a design-led build.
fails: Values tuned by eye against one viewport size break at others unless re-checked responsively.

claim: For a text-reveal wipe, animate the mask/overlay element's width between 0 and 100% rather than moving the text itself; keep the text stationary and let the covering block change size.
why: Sizing a single overlay is cheaper to reason about than translating text, and it lets the reveal edge sweep across without the type ever shifting position.
when: Building a wipe-style reveal for headings or word-level text in a loader or hero intro.

claim: Control which edge a width-animated wipe grows from or collapses toward by pinning the element with a single absolute offset: `left: 0` anchors the sweep to start at the left, `right: 0` makes it retreat toward the right.
why: An absolutely positioned block expands away from whichever edge it is pinned to, so the pinned edge is the fixed one and the free edge is what sweeps.
when: A two-stage wipe where the cover comes in from one side and must exit from the opposite side, so the anchor has to change partway through the sequence.
fails: If both offsets are simultaneously non-auto the element becomes stretched between both edges and the width animation is ignored — one side must be released.

claim: When flipping an absolutely positioned element's anchor, explicitly reset the old offset to `auto` (e.g. set `left: auto` when introducing `right: 0`) rather than relying on the new value to override it.
why: The previously applied offset persists as an inline or computed value and keeps constraining the element, so the new anchor silently does nothing until the old one is released.
when: Mid-timeline anchor changes in JS-driven animation, where earlier tween steps have already written offsets onto the element's inline style.
fails: Unnecessary when the element was never given the opposing offset in the first place — an extra property with no effect.

claim: Set the revealed text to opacity 1 in the same timeline step that opens the mask, rather than leaving visibility to the mask alone.
why: The text is held hidden before the sequence so it never flashes during layout or the first frames; the reveal step is the moment to hand visibility back.
when: Any staged intro where content must be invisible until its cue.

claim: Use an ease-in-out exponential curve with roughly a one-second duration for full-width wipe sweeps.
why: Exponential in-out starts and ends near-still with a fast middle, which makes a large-distance sweep read as deliberate and premium rather than linear or mechanical.
when: Large-travel reveal elements in a premium loading or intro sequence.
fails: Too slow and heavy for small UI feedback like hovers or button states, where shorter durations and gentler curves suit better.

claim: Reveal text with a wipe by animating a covering block's width from full to 0% rather than fading the text's opacity — the block uncovers the letters as it retracts.
why: A geometric mask retracting produces a directional, mechanical reveal that reads as deliberate craft, whereas an opacity fade reads as generic and gives no sense of direction.
when: Revealing headline or hero text in an intro/load sequence where you want a premium, directional entrance.
fails: The overlay colour must match what sits behind the text; over a photo, gradient, or transparent background the solid block becomes visible as a rectangle instead of disappearing into the surface.

claim: Give every tween in a single load sequence the same duration and the same easing curve unless you have a specific reason to differentiate.
why: Shared timing and easing make separate elements feel driven by one physical system; mismatched curves make a sequence feel assembled from unrelated parts.
when: Building a multi-step load or intro timeline where the steps should read as one continuous motion.
fails: When elements are meant to be hierarchically distinct — a primary element that should lead and a secondary that trails benefit from deliberately different durations.

claim: Use an expo in-out curve for wipe and mask reveals of roughly one second, so the block starts slow, crosses the text fast, and settles slow.
why: The steep middle of an exponential curve keeps the overlay from lingering over the text at the moment it would be most obstructive, while the eased ends prevent a hard start and stop.
when: Full-width or full-height masking elements travelling across content during an entrance animation.
fails: On small, frequently repeated micro-interactions, where an expo curve's long slow tails feel sluggish and a shorter linear-ish or out-only ease serves better.

claim: Build the entire load sequence as a paused timeline and call play as an explicit final step, rather than letting each tween fire on creation.
why: Assembling first and triggering last lets you control exactly when the sequence begins — after fonts, images, or a preloader resolve — and keeps the whole animation replayable and scrubbable as a single object.
when: Any multi-tween page-load or intro animation.

claim: Verify a load animation by hard-refreshing the page and watching it run at full speed, not by inspecting the timeline in isolation.
why: Load animations only exist in the first seconds of a page's life; timing problems, flashes of unstyled content, and overlays that reveal too early only surface in a real cold load.
when: Every time you add or change a tween in an on-load sequence.

claim: Design button hover feedback by moving duplicated label text through a clipped mask, revealing the alternate label position as the pointer enters.
why: Motion communicates the state change while preserving the button’s visual system, avoiding the need to invent additional hover colors.
when: A button has a text label and benefits from a compact, polished hover response.
fails: The moving label harms readability, clips essential information, or conflicts with reduced-motion requirements.

claim: Add a subtle scale-down animation to a button’s pressed state to make the click feel tactile.
why: A brief compression visually confirms that the control is being pressed.
when: Interactive buttons need immediate press feedback.
fails: The scale change causes layout shifts, makes nearby controls move, or is too large to feel like a physical press.

claim: Vary the direction of hover movement—vertical, horizontal, or diagonal—while keeping the interaction understandable.
why: The same masked-text pattern can produce distinct visual character without adding color-state complexity.
when: Adapting a button interaction to a product’s visual language.
fails: Directional motion is inconsistent with surrounding controls or obscures the label transition.

claim: When an interface supports a keyboard shortcut, pair its activation with a short, distinctive confirmation animation or success message.
why: A visible reward after successful use gives the shortcut a memorable interaction signature, making it less likely to be forgotten.
when: A shortcut performs a meaningful action and users may need reinforcement that they triggered it correctly.
fails: The animation is overly frequent, slow, or distracting enough to interrupt repeated expert use.

claim: In prototypes, replace unsupported modifier-key inputs with clearly chosen substitute keys so the interaction can still be demonstrated.
why: Prototype-tool limitations should not prevent testing or presenting the shortcut’s feedback behavior.
when: The design tool cannot bind the exact production shortcut combination.
fails: The substitute keys are presented as the final product shortcut rather than a prototype-only stand-in.

claim: Treat a toast as a compact stateful feedback component: pair its entrance motion with an animation that reflects the current outcome, such as loading or success.
