why: State-specific movement makes the feedback card feel more informative and engaging than a generic notification.
when: A transient notification represents an action that is pending, completed, or otherwise has a meaningful status.
fails: Overly decorative motion distracts from urgent, error, or high-frequency notifications.

claim: Use a delayed trigger to sequence secondary toast details after its initial entrance, rather than animating every element simultaneously.
why: Staggering creates a clearer progression from notification arrival to status detail or celebration.
when: A toast contains multiple animated layers, such as a card entrance followed by an indicator or particles.

claim: Use click triggers for toast interactions that should respond directly to the user.
why: Direct manipulation makes the small card feel interactive rather than purely passive.
when: The toast includes an actionable or dismissible interaction.

claim: When showing small avatars or headshots, reveal a compact name tag on hover so identity is available without permanently crowding the interface.
why: Small images alone may not identify people clearly; an on-demand label preserves a minimal default layout while supplying context.
when: User-facing profile images are small and hover is available, such as team, agency, or collaborator displays.
fails: Touch-first interfaces lack a dependable hover state, so the identity must be available through another interaction or visible text.

claim: Build hover labels as matching elements in two component states, changing only position and visibility, so Smart Animate can interpolate the transition cleanly.
why: Using the same tag in each frame lets the prototype animate it as one object rather than swapping abruptly between unrelated layers.
when: Prototyping a hover reveal in Figma with Smart Animate.

claim: Use a dark label with white text, fully rounded corners, and compact Auto Layout padding for a legible tooltip-like name tag.
why: The demonstrated styling produces a small, self-contained label that stays readable over varied page content.
when: The label needs to be visually distinct and unobtrusive near an avatar.
fails: A dark fill lacks sufficient contrast against the surrounding design or conflicts with the established color system.

claim: Hide the resting tag by offsetting it slightly downward and setting opacity to zero, then animate it into its final position on hover.
why: Combining translation with a fade creates a pop-out motion rather than a sudden appearance.
when: A hover label should feel lightweight and spatially connected to its trigger.

claim: Tune hover motion with a custom spring rather than accepting a generic transition when the intended character of the animation matters.
why: The chapter attributes the perceptible difference in animation feel to the custom easing settings.
when: Creating a refined microinteraction in Figma.
fails: Strict motion-system requirements, accessibility constraints, or platform conventions prescribe different timing and easing.

claim: Build an animated border as a hollow shape, then use it as a mask for a separately animated gradient layer.
why: Separating the visible border geometry from the color animation makes a continuous shimmer possible without animating the outline itself.
when: A component needs a decorative, modern gradient stroke in a prototype or interface.

claim: Use an angular gradient and rotate it to create a looping shimmer around a bordered shape.
why: Rotating the gradient changes which colors are visible through the fixed masked outline, creating the illusion of light traveling around it.
when: The desired motion should circulate around an outline rather than sweep linearly across a surface.

claim: Assess perceived speed around the whole border before shipping a rotating-gradient effect, because corners and side segments may feel faster than horizontal segments.
why: The demonstrated construction produces non-uniform shimmer movement along different portions of the rectangular outline.
when: Using a circular angular-gradient source masked into a non-circular border.
fails: A uniform-speed border animation is required.

claim: Provide a pause/play control for decorative animation when users may find its motion distracting.
why: Playback control lets people opt out of an aesthetic effect whose uneven or continuous motion may not suit them.
when: A visible shimmer runs continuously or could affect concentration.

claim: Attach a contextual visual reveal to a text hover when a label needs explanation or demonstration but the base layout should stay compact.
why: The reveal lets the interface show the subject of the text without permanently consuming space with additional words or images.
when: A desktop or pointer-based interface has short labels, links, or feature names that benefit from on-demand visual context.
fails: On touch-first interfaces or for essential information that must be visible without hover.

claim: Build the effect from a hover interaction between frames, keeping the pop-out elements inside the hover state.
why: A frame-level hover state provides a straightforward way to swap from resting text to text plus the revealed content.
when: Prototyping the interaction in Figma or implementing a discrete hover state in a UI.

claim: Favor a playful, lightweight visual treatment for hover pop-outs so exploration feels rewarding rather than disruptive.
why: The described examples and the presenter’s reaction position the interaction as an enjoyable micro-detail.
when: The brand and task allow expressive interaction feedback.
fails: Dense productivity flows, accessibility-sensitive contexts, or interfaces that require restrained motion.

claim: Animate progress indicators during multi-step forms to provide engaging, continuous feedback instead of leaving progress visually static.
why: Smooth progress motion helps make an otherwise tedious form experience feel more active.
when: A user is completing a multi-step flow, onboarding sequence, or other unavoidable form.

claim: In Figma, create a path-drawing progress animation by placing the progress stroke inside a mask and sliding a colored rectangle across it.
why: The moving mask progressively reveals the stroke, producing the illusion that the line is being drawn.
when: Animating linear or curved progress paths, including paths that wrap around circles.
fails: When the desired motion requires a changing path shape rather than a progressive reveal.

claim: Keep secondary progress-state changes understated by fading elements in and out.
why: Fades support the primary drawing motion without competing with it.
when: Additional labels, states, or decorative elements appear or disappear around a progress animation.

claim: When dismissing the front card in a stacked-card UI, animate it with both a directional rotation and opacity fade to zero.
why: The combination clearly communicates that the card is being swiped away rather than simply disappearing.
when: A user removes a foreground card from a compact stack, such as notifications or image cards.

claim: As the front card leaves, scale the cards behind upward and shift them downward to promote them through the stack.
why: Advancing the background cards preserves the sense of a continuous ordered deck.
when: Cards overlap in depth and the next item should become the primary visible item.

claim: Start moving the cards behind while the user drags the front card so they fill its vacated space in real time.
why: Responsive displacement makes the stack appear to move forward physically and completes the interaction illusion.
when: The dismissal is drag-driven and cards visibly overlap.
fails: The cards are independent list items with no stacked-depth relationship.

claim: Adapt an interaction pattern’s placement to the surrounding product context while retaining its core behavior.
why: The same card-swipe mechanic can serve different roles, such as a sidebar feed or bottom-right notification center.
when: Reusing a familiar motion pattern in a different layout.

claim: Collapse nonessential search inputs into a recognizable magnifying-glass trigger, then reveal the full field only after the user activates it.
why: This preserves screen space and reduces the visual weight of a search bar until search is needed.
when: Search is a secondary action and the magnifying-glass convention is appropriate for the audience.
fails: Search is a primary, frequent task that benefits from a persistently visible input.

claim: Make the search icon visually merge into the expanding search container during the opening transition.
why: A continuous visual handoff makes the state change feel deliberate rather than like two unrelated elements swapping places.
when: Animating a compact icon into a larger search control.

claim: Prototype the expansion as a small sequence of states triggered by click, with a short intermediary delay before the final expanded state.
why: A lightweight multi-frame sequence can produce a polished transition without complex animation setup.
when: Building the interaction in Figma or another state-based prototyping tool.

claim: On hover over a plan limit or upgrade affordance, reveal the upgraded allowance through a short slide-in transition.
why: The motion makes the upgrade benefit discoverable without permanently adding detail to the default interface.
when: A compact pricing, usage-limit, or entitlement UI needs to communicate what a higher tier unlocks.
fails: The upgrade information must be visible for comprehension or accessibility without pointer hover.

claim: Replace a strikethrough-and-replacement treatment for changing limits with a clean incoming value and outgoing current value.
why: A direct transition communicates the new state while avoiding the cluttered or awkward appearance of crossed-out text.
when: A hover state compares a current allowance with an upgraded allowance in a small UI element.
fails: The design specifically needs to preserve the old value as a deliberate before-versus-after comparison.

claim: Keep upgrade-preview micro-interactions restrained: one state change and one clear motion cue are sufficient.
why: The demonstrated interaction is intentionally simple, yet still adds consideration and polish.
when: Adding feedback to an existing control or metric without distracting from the surrounding interface.
fails: Users need multiple plan differences, detailed pricing, or a persistent comparison view.

claim: Prototype a full-page loading reveal with two matched screen states: one covered by a branded overlay and one exposing the finished page.
why: Duplicating the page preserves a consistent destination layout while the overlay supplies a clear loading state to animate away.
when: A site needs a branded transition before its initial content is revealed.

claim: Make the loading overlay cover the entire viewport and center a brand mark within it.
why: A complete cover prevents early content exposure and gives the loading moment a deliberate focal point.
when: Creating a minimal branded loading screen.

claim: Prepare elements for entrance animation by setting their initial visibility to zero and offsetting them from their final positions.
why: Figma needs distinct start and end states for opacity and movement to interpolate an entrance.
when: Animating navigation and page content into view after a loader clears.

claim: When a loading panel exits vertically, move the content it reveals in the same direction during the transition.
why: Shared motion makes the handoff from loading state to completed screen read as one intentional animation rather than disconnected layers.
when: A loading, splash, or overlay panel slides away to reveal an interface beneath it.
fails: The intended effect is for the revealed content to remain spatially fixed or deliberately contrast the overlay's motion.

claim: Use duplicated frames to isolate each meaningful animation state: initial loading, loader exit with centered content, then navigation reveal.
why: Separate states allow Figma's prototype interpolation to animate only the properties that change between each phase.
when: Creating staged interface animations in Figma without a dedicated timeline.

claim: Delay the transition from the initial loading state by about one second, then run the navigation transition for about 800 ms with a custom eased curve.
why: A brief hold establishes the loading state, while eased movement makes the outgoing panel feel less mechanical.
when: Prototyping this particular polished loading-screen reveal.
fails: The product requires faster feedback, reduced motion, or a duration dictated by real loading progress.

claim: Reveal navigation only after the main loading-panel transition has reached its final layout.
why: Staggering the nav prevents competing visual changes and gives the content reveal a clear sequence.
when: A navigation bar is initially hidden behind or alongside a loading experience.

claim: For a navigation element that should arrive after the rest of a screen, add a small delay before its opacity-based Smart Animate transition, then use an ease-in-out curve for the reveal.
why: A delayed, eased entrance makes the navigation appear intentionally sequenced rather than abruptly present.
when: A secondary navigation area should enter after the main loading or page content.

claim: Use short transition durations for small UI reveals so they feel responsive; the demonstrated navigation fade uses 200 ms.
why: Small interface elements do not need a long animation to communicate their arrival.
when: Animating a simple fade-in of compact navigation controls.

claim: Build an expanding component animation from duplicated frames that represent its expanded and collapsed endpoint states.
why: Figma Smart Animate can interpolate matching layers between near-identical frame copies.
when: Creating a component that changes size between two stable layouts, such as an expandable navigation bar.
fails: The states do not preserve corresponding layers or require a discontinuous structural change.

claim: Make content invisible in the collapsed starting state, then reduce the container to the intended compact dimensions before animating toward the full state.
why: The compact state needs to contain only the visible trigger while the rest of the navigation is concealed until expansion.
when: An expanded control begins as a compact icon-sized button.

claim: Model a loading sequence as a series of duplicate frames whose only differences are the properties being animated.
why: Keeping most content identical lets Figma interpolate the intended changes cleanly and makes the sequence easier to inspect.
when: Creating a prototype animation from static UI elements in Figma.
fails: The transition requires fundamentally different layout structure or independently controlled interactive states.

claim: Reveal interface elements progressively by setting them transparent in earlier frames and fully opaque in the frame where they should appear.
why: Opacity-based state changes create controlled entrances without removing the element from the visual composition.
when: Staging a logo, menu, button, or other loader content into view.
fails: The hidden element must not occupy its original layout space or should be inaccessible before appearing.

claim: Use an initial timed instant transition to hold the first loading state before motion begins.
why: A short pause establishes the starting state before subsequent animated reveals.
when: A loader or intro needs a deliberate beat before the animation starts.
fails: The experience must react immediately to user input or cannot tolerate an artificial delay.

claim: Use Smart Animate with an ease-in-out curve for a straightforward element entrance, then use a custom Bézier curve when a more accelerated motion character is needed.
why: Different timing curves control whether motion feels even and gentle or more dramatically accelerating.
when: Tuning the perceived energy of sequential loading-animation transitions.
fails: A consistent motion system requires the same easing across all transitions.

claim: Use the same transition configuration across related loading or navigation animations: a 1 ms delay, 200 ms Smart Animate transition, and ease-in-out easing.
why: Shared timing makes separate interface elements enter as one coherent motion system.
when: Several adjacent UI elements, such as navbar contents, should reveal with a consistent feel.
fails: Elements need intentionally different hierarchy, timing, or interaction feedback.

claim: Create a text-wipe effect by animating a thin coloured rectangle across text while switching the text’s opacity between hidden and visible across duplicated frames.
why: The moving rectangle acts as the visible wipe while opacity states control when the final text is revealed.
when: A label or heading needs a simple directional loading or reveal animation in Figma.
fails: The wipe needs to reveal individual glyphs, follow irregular shapes, or support responsive text reflow without rebuilding the states.

claim: Make the wipe rectangle at least as tall as the text and begin with a very narrow width before moving it across the label.
why: A narrow, text-covering bar produces a clean sweep rather than looking like a large panel transition.
when: The wipe moves horizontally over a single line of text.
fails: The text spans multiple lines or the intended motion is vertical or shape-based.

claim: Build a loading animation as a chain of separate state frames connected by timed prototype interactions.
why: Individual frames make each visual state controllable while Figma supplies the playback sequence.
when: A loader or micro-animation consists of distinct text, shape, or layout states that can be represented as frames.

claim: Set the first state as the prototype starting point before configuring the sequence.
why: The prototype needs a defined entry frame to play the animation from the intended state.
when: Creating a standalone prototype flow or animation with multiple possible frames.

claim: Use instant navigation for deliberate state changes that should not visibly interpolate.
why: An instant handoff preserves a discrete jump between states and avoids unintended motion.
when: Moving between loader stages that should appear as a swap rather than a transition.
fails: The visual change should read as continuous movement or morphing.

claim: Use Smart Animate between matching consecutive states when elements should transition smoothly.
why: It interpolates changes across frames, producing visible motion rather than a hard cut.
when: Corresponding layers persist across frames and their properties or positions change.
fails: Layers cannot be matched reliably or a discontinuous change is intended.

claim: Tune loading-animation pacing with explicit trigger delays, transition durations, and a custom easing curve.
why: Timing controls the rhythm of state changes, while easing determines the perceived acceleration and deceleration.
when: The default prototype motion does not match the intended energetic or polished feel.

claim: Use Smart Animate with an explicit custom duration when adjacent prototype states should interpolate smoothly.
why: A defined duration makes the transition’s pacing intentional and allows Figma to animate matching properties between states.
when: Two frames or component variants share layers whose changed properties should animate between matching states.
fails: The transition needs to be a discrete jump rather than interpolated motion.

claim: Use an almost-immediate delayed instant transition to advance a loading sequence to its terminal state without adding visible motion.
why: The tiny delay preserves sequence order while the instant action avoids an unnecessary final tween.
when: A prototype must trigger a final state immediately after the preceding animation completes.
fails: The final change should be perceptible as part of the animation rather than a state handoff.

claim: Preview the complete prototype after wiring its last transitions to validate the motion as a single sequence.
why: Individual transition settings need end-to-end playback to confirm the timing and order feel correct together.
when: A multi-step loading or state-based animation has been assembled.

claim: Animate elements to direct attention to the product and reveal it early in the section.
why: Motion earns its place when it gives viewers a clear first look at what the product is and does.
when: A landing-page section needs to introduce a product, feature, or interface.
fails: The animation withholds the product until later merely to create suspense or visual flair.

claim: Coordinate scroll transitions so outgoing supporting content recedes while the product interface becomes prominent.
why: A deliberate handoff from copy to interface creates a clear visual hierarchy during the section transition.
when: Using scroll-linked motion to move a viewer from explanatory text into a product demonstration.
fails: The transition causes competing elements, unclear focus, or distracts from the content being introduced.

claim: Prefer the simplest interaction that demonstrates the product behavior, such as a purposeful hover state, over elaborate animation sequences.
why: A compact demonstration can make the product understandable while preserving easy navigation.
when: The product interaction can be communicated in one focused visual response.
fails: The needed behavior cannot be meaningfully conveyed by a small interaction alone.

claim: Treat navigation and comprehension as constraints on animation complexity.
why: Decorative motion that makes movement through the page harder provides little value and harms usability.
when: Adding or evaluating animations in marketing and product pages.

claim: Break an established layout or interaction pattern sparingly with a purposeful surprise.
why: A well-executed unexpected moment renews attention, while repeated novelty would compete with clarity.
when: A user has learned the current visual rhythm and you need to transition to an important new message or feature group.
fails: The surprise distracts from comprehension, feels gratuitous, or occurs so often that it becomes the new pattern.

claim: Use a transition point where users expect an animation or section to end as an opportunity to reveal supporting content.
why: The violated expectation makes the continuation feel engaging and gives the new information a natural entrance.
when: An existing product or interface animation has reached a satisfying apparent endpoint.
fails: The continuation delays a task, hides essential controls, or makes the interaction feel longer without adding value.

claim: Keep surprise animations visually contained: reduce competing UI and move in simple copy rather than adding many simultaneous effects.
why: Restrained motion preserves clarity while avoiding a generic static image-and-text composition.
when: Introducing a high-level feature explanation after an interactive visual demonstration.
fails: The message requires persistent UI context or users need to compare the text with detailed interface elements.

claim: Use alignment and typographic contrast to distinguish interactive commands, supporting labels, and keyboard shortcuts without requiring extra explanation.
why: A menu becomes scannable when visual hierarchy tells users which elements can be acted on and which elements provide context.
when: Designing dense command menus, settings lists, contextual menus, or other interfaces with multiple item roles.
fails: If contrast is so strong that secondary information becomes hard to read or visually competes with the primary command.

claim: Add a small, relevant interaction surprise after a user selects an interface element to make exploration feel rewarding.
why: A well-crafted transition or expanded surface gives positive feedback and makes a previously static area feel alive.
when: Opening menus, dialogs, detail views, or other moments where a user has intentionally engaged with the UI.
fails: When the effect delays completion, distracts from a critical task, or is inconsistent with the interaction’s importance.

claim: Keep onboarding screens visually focused before introducing controls or complexity.
why: A clean initial structure directs attention to the current step and makes later revealed tools easier to understand.
when: Guiding first-time users through a mobile or web-app onboarding sequence.
fails: When users need immediate access to essential controls to complete the task safely or efficiently.

claim: Make animation direction reflect the interface meaning: upward movement can signal a temporary action surface, while lateral screen movement can communicate progression through a sequence.
why: Spatial motion helps users form a mental model of where a surface comes from and whether they are advancing through a flow.
when: Animating bottom sheets, temporary editors, step-based onboarding, or other layered navigation states.
fails: When the chosen direction conflicts with an established platform convention or the product’s existing navigation model.

claim: Use animation to orient users, not only to decorate the interface.
why: The demonstrated transitions clarify the relationship between the current screen, temporary tools, and the next onboarding state.
when: Introducing new controls, changing context, or moving users through a multi-step flow.
fails: When motion adds no state information and merely creates delay or visual noise.

claim: Add subtle, slow scale animation to images when you want a polished sense of life without distracting from content.
why: Small zoom changes create movement while preserving a refined visual tone.
when: Decorative or editorial image areas where the image remains legible throughout motion.
fails: The movement competes with reading, obscures important image detail, or creates unnecessary distraction.

claim: Use interaction-dependent components such as accordions to let users reveal supporting information on demand.
why: They turn information disclosure into an active, compact experience.
when: Content can be grouped into independent, clearly labeled sections.
fails: Critical information is hidden from users who may not discover or operate the control.

claim: Evaluate motion-heavy patterns, including marquees, against their usability cost before adopting them.
why: A visually trendy animated section can make content harder to scan, access, or control.
when: Considering continuously moving text or other attention-grabbing animated treatments.
